paragraphs.text: The voyage began as many such voyages do. The air quivered with excitement, adventure, and a sense of mystery as my fellow passengers and I boarded the transatlantic steamship Provence . We enjoyed making each other's acquaintance, and though we were sociable and charming, we kept the safe distance that characterizes those who may never see each other again. Here, on this ship, we had the luxury of being isolated from the world, except for one inescapable link—the wireless telegraph. Its voice followed us around like an ever-present shadow, whispering words of the outside world. I was the recipient of two telegrams. Others, too, received messages from family and friends wishing them bon voyage .

However, on the second day of our voyage, we received a telegram so startling and vicious, it destroyed the peace we had enjoyed up until that moment. It read: Caution! Arsène Lupin is aboard the Provence. First-class cabin, blond hair, wound on right forearm. Traveling alone under the name of R—

At that most crucial moment, a flash of lightning interrupted the transmission, and the rest of the message never reached us. The passengers only knew Lupin was using an alias beginning with the letter R .

That, however, was enough to rouse fear and apprehension among everyone on board the ship. Arsène Lupin! The infamous gentleman burglar's exploits were well reported in newspapers across France and in other European countries.
"Horrible! Arsène Lupin is in our midst!" exclaimed Miss Nelly Underdown, the prettiest woman on the ship and—dare I say—loveliest of all lovely creatures on land.

"They say Lupin is a man of a thousand faces," I said. "He could appear as a chauffeur or a Russian physician, a Spanish bullfighter or an old man. No one can say for certain what Lupin truly looks like. He is a master of disguise."
"You do not put one's mind at ease," lamented Lady Jerland, who was Miss Nelly's traveling companion. "How are we to secure our valuables?"
A group of us had gathered on the rear deck of the ship, reclining comfortably on lounge chairs. The day was bright and warm, with no sign of the storm that had interrupted the notorious telegram.
"How can we protect ourselves from this madman?" cried Miss Nelly.
"I would hardly call Lupin a madman," I said, trying to comfort her and gently placing my hand on her shoulder. She lowered her eyes and blushed.
"Monsieur d'Andrézy," said Miss Nelly, "you are on such intimate terms with the captain. Surely you know something?"
I laughed, delighted by Miss Nelly's confidence in me.

"I assure you, I have no definite knowledge," I replied. "But can't we investigate this matter just as well as Detective Ganimard, the personal enemy of Arsène Lupin?" It was common knowledge that Ganimard had vowed to bring Lupin to justice, even if he had to follow Lupin to the ends of the earth.
"It sounds a bit complicated," said Miss Nelly.
"Lupin's vocation, though unsavory to many, does take a certain amount of skill. Every movement detailed and timed to the second—"
"If I may be so bold as to speak," interrupted Monsieur Rozaine, a young man who rivaled me for the affections of Miss Nelly earlier, "it appears that you admire Lupin, Monsieur Bernard d'Andrézy."
Ignoring his comment, I continued. "Lupin's skill demonstrates not the work of a madman, Miss Nelly, but the art of a clever, organized, and very meticulous person."
"But then who could ever catch such a man?" Miss Nelly sighed, her full lips in a pout.

I took a moment to reflect on the exquisite Miss Nelly, with her golden hair and deep emerald eyes. Her skin was like porcelain, and her body was as perfectly proportioned as that of Venus, the goddess of beauty.
"My dear, all this dreadful talk has left me quite weak," Lady Jerland murmured. "I shall retire to my quarters to lie down before tea."
I waited patiently until Lady Jerland left before going on.
"Although we might not be quite as resourceful as the celebrated Detective Ganimard, we do have some facts to help us determine who Lupin may be."
"Please explain, Monsieur d'Andrézy," pleaded Miss Nelly.
"With pleasure," I said, bowing, and removed a passenger list from my right pocket. Using my left hand to unfold the paper took a few moments, and everyone patiently waited for me to resume.
"First, Lupin is using an alias beginning with R ," I reminded them.
"That's a common letter for a surname," argued Rozaine.
"Second, he is traveling alone," I noted.
"So are half the passengers on this ship," Rozaine interjected. Miss Nelly nodded vigorously in agreement, and Rozaine's face lit up.
"Third, he is blond." I smiled at everyone.
"Well?" Rozaine shrugged his shoulders.
"Well, now it is a matter of process of elimination," I said. "Here, on this passenger list, there are only thirteen men with surnames that begin with R , and nine are family men."
"That leaves just four who are traveling alone," calculated Miss Nelly.
"Correct, mademoiselle," I nodded. "Of the four, one is the Marquis de Raverdan—"
"He is the secretary to the American ambassador," interrupted Miss Nelly. "I know him well."
I scrolled down the list. "The second is Major Rawson."
"He's my uncle," someone else called out.
"Monsieur Rivolta is the third," I said.
"That's me," exclaimed a dark Italian with a heavy, black beard.
"You can hardly be called a blond," said Miss Nelly.
"And finally"—I paused before continuing—"Monsieur Rozaine."
All eyes fixed on the young, blond-haired man. He turned red and was rendered speechless.
"Well, Monsieur Rozaine? Have you anything to say?" Miss Nelly demanded of him.
"This is insanity!" Rozaine finally cried. He struggled to his feet. Some of the women recoiled in terror.
"I admit I fit the description of that scoundrel Lupin, but I swear I am not he," Rozaine shouted excitedly.
"Didn't the telegram say something about a wound?" asked Miss Nelly.
Everyone nodded and began murmuring.
"I can prove to you I have no such wound," sputtered Rozaine, rolling up his left shirtsleeve.

Smiling secretly, I remembered the wound was said to be on his right arm, not on his left. I was about to call attention to that fact when a loud scream erupted from the sleeping quarters. Everyone abandoned the deck and rushed to the inner part of the ship.
"Help, help!" Lady Jerland wailed frantically. Her cheeks were smeared with makeup and tears. She was breathing heavily. "They're gone! My jewels! My pearls! They're gone!"

I led the way into Lady Jerland's cabin. Pieces of jewelry still lay on top of her dresser; the thief had taken only the most precious diamonds and pearls and left the rest. Each stolen jewel had been carefully removed from its mounting.
"Yes, Lady Jerland's unblemished pearls were indeed a prize," I whispered to Miss Nelly.
"Who could have done this?" Lady Jerland wept bitterly.
The passengers looked at one another. They had all reached the same conclusion. This was the work of Arsène Lupin.

I have attempted to relate in detail the affairs aboard the Provence thus far. In light of the circumstances, I was not surprised that, after Lady Jerland’s jewels were stolen, all eyes shifted to Monsieur Rozaine. Everyone thought the captain would detain Rozaine (who surely had to be Lupin) for the remainder of the voyage. But to our amazement, the next day Rozaine was walking around a free man.
"What do you mean he’s been released?" barked Lady Jerland.
"His documents show that he is who he says he is," I explained. "And he did not have a wound on his right arm. The captain had no evidence to arrest him."
"Documents!" exclaimed Lady Jerland. "Lupin could furnish as many documents as might be desired!"
Soon after the theft, Rozaine announced a reward of ten thousand francs for the capture of Lupin. "If no one assists me," declared Rozaine, "I will find the scoundrel myself."
"Ah, Rozaine against Arsène Lupin, or rather, according to popular opinion, Arsène Lupin against himself," I thought. "The contest promises to be interesting."
The captain and crew displayed admirable tenacity as they ransacked every cabin, leaving no stone unturned. The jewels had to be concealed somewhere aboard ship.
All was quiet for the next few days. Miss Nelly and I watched as Rozaine searched everywhere, even in the life jackets stored under the lifeboats.
"What does he hope to find?" whispered Miss Nelly. "Does Lupin have magical powers to shrink himself to the size of a rat? Or would he be foolish enough to hide the jewels in plain view?"

"If I were Rozaine, I would examine the lining of our hats, the hems of skirts, and everything we carry with us," I said, holding up my camera as an example. "Within a device as compact as this, a person could hide jewels. He could pretend to take pictures and nobody would suspect a thing."
"But even the cleverest of thieves must leave some clue behind," Miss Nelly insisted.
"Generally speaking, perhaps," I replied. "But with one exception: Lupin."
"Why must he be excluded?" demanded Miss Nelly.

"Because most thieves concentrate on the theft and carelessly leave behind some trace of themselves. Lupin, however, focuses on all the circumstances that could somehow serve as a clue to his identity," I explained. "That is why no one has been able to catch him. They don’t know who he is!"
"Earlier you were so confident that you could discover the identity of Lupin, Monsieur d’Andrézy," Miss Nelly remarked.
"Indeed, I was," I admitted, "but since I have seen him at work, I think we are wasting our time."

The investigation into Lady Jerland’s stolen jewels resulted in disappointment. In the meantime the captain’s watch was stolen too. Furious, the captain once again turned his attention to Rozaine. The next evening, however, Rozaine’s claim of innocence was justified. An officer on deck heard groans coming from under the lifeboats. He found Rozaine tied up, his head wrapped in a scarf, and with a card that revealed the perpetrator pinned to his coat. It read: Arsène Lupin gladly accepts the ten thousand francs offered by Monsieur Rozaine. As for the captain, he should ask his second officer for the time of day. Rozaine’s wallet was empty, and the captain later found his watch inside the officer’s quarters.
Arsène Lupin was now anybody and everybody. Fear permeated the ship as people prayed for the remainder of the voyage to pass without further incident.

I, on the other hand, was probably the only passenger to benefit from the near-panic on the ship. It brought Miss Nelly and me closer together. She was afraid and mistrusted others, so I availed myself of her companionship throughout the ordeal. Miss Nelly and I shared many delightful hours together. She spoke fondly of her world travels, and I took photos of her with my camera.
And now we waited anxiously as the Provence approached the shores of America.

"Monsieur d’Andrézy," Miss Nelly cried breathlessly, "it appears we have a welcoming committee." She pointed to a group of uniformed officers standing on the dock. As the Provence pulled in, the officers separated to allow one man to walk through. I gasped.
"You are pale, monsieur." Miss Nelly grabbed my right arm. I flinched but managed to suppress a cry of pain.
"Do you see that little man?" I pointed and then handed my camera to her.
"The one wearing the green coat and carrying an umbrella?" said Miss Nelly.
"That very one. He is the famous Detective Ganimard," I replied.
"Ganimard?" repeated Miss Nelly.
"Yes, the detective who has dedicated his life to capturing Arsène Lupin," I continued. "That can mean only one thing . . ."
"He will arrest Lupin?" Miss Nelly asked excitedly.
I shrugged. "No doubt Lupin already knows his enemy is here. He will be in no hurry to leave the ship."
The passengers walked down the gangway, but Ganimard appeared to pay no attention to the crowd disembarking from the ship. Even Rozaine walked off without a glance from the detective.

"Who could Lupin be?" Miss Nelly wondered aloud, scrutinizing the few faces that remained on deck. The captain signaled for Miss Nelly and me to walk down the gangway next. We had not taken more than ten steps when Ganimard blocked our way.
"A moment, please," he said.
"What is the meaning of this, officer?" I demanded.
"You know well what the meaning is"—here Ganimard paused—"Monsieur Lupin."
I laughed loudly. "You are mistaken, sir. I am Bernard d’Andrézy. I believe Lupin was sailing under a name beginning with R ."
Ganimard smiled coldly. "That telegram was a clever trick. It deceived everyone but me. I am well acquainted with your tactics, Lupin, and now your time is up."
"Stop," Miss Nelly said. "Monsieur d’Andrézy is a gentleman."
"Bernard d’Andrézy died three years ago," said Ganimard, and he raised his umbrella and struck my right arm with it.
I cried out in pain. The wound had not yet healed and began to bleed again. I had no choice but to surrender.

"Yes, I am the man you are looking for. However, what evidence do you have that I committed any crime?" I turned to Miss Nelly. Our eyes locked, and she glanced at the camera in her hand. She now understood what was inside the camera.
"I am confident we will find what we are looking for," Ganimard said, his face close to mine.

Miss Nelly walked past the detective and me, and then suddenly she seemed to trip. Faking awkwardness, she let the camera fall into the water between the ship and the pier. Then she walked down the gangway and was quickly lost in the crowd. She had passed out of my life forever.
I turned to Ganimard and said, "It is indeed a shame that I am not an honest man."

This is the story Arsène Lupin told me of his arrest. We are friends, and he occasionally comes to see me, bringing his youthful spirit with him. I have seen him twenty times, and each time, he is a different person. As I sit here organizing my notes, I plan to one day publish the affairs of this gentleman burglar. I hope the public will be able to refer to my work and say: "Arsène Lupin did that!" Now let me share with you what happened to Lupin in prison.

On a rock in the middle of the Seine River sits a little manor called Malaquis Castle. Connected to the mainland only by an arched bridge, Malaquis Castle has been surrounded by intrigue and menace since it was built. Many legends surround the mysterious castle. One legend tells of a famous tunnel that supposedly led to an abbey and the house of a lover of a French king. A most eccentric millionaire, Baron Cahorn, lived alone in the castle with his treasures and three old servants. He lived in constant fear, but not in fear for his life, oh no; he feared that his private collection of antique furniture, rare art, and wood carvings would be stolen. So he barricaded himself in the castle and, every day at sunset, locked the iron gates at each end of the bridge. The baron guarded his private art collection as possessively and passionately as a jealous lover.
One September day a man with merry eyes and a pleasant manner showed up at one gate with some newspapers.
"Good morning, Baron Cahorn," the man said in a friendly voice.
Partially opening the gate, the baron scrutinized the man as if he had never seen him before.
"Why are you looking at me like that?" said the man, laughing. "It is only I—the postman who comes every day."
"One can never be too sure about who people are," muttered the baron.
The baron took the newspapers and was about to close the gate when the postman exclaimed, "Oh, here is something new, Baron." The postman handed him a thin envelope.
"For me?"
Having no intimate friends or business relations, the baron seldom, if ever, received any letters. So he reacted to this occurrence with both suspicion and alarm.
"It’s a registered letter, sir. Please sign here," said the postman.

Baron Cahorn signed, took the letter, and watched as the man tipped his cap and disappeared down the road, whistling an aria from The Magic Flute . Then, leaning against the gate, he tore open the letter. It contained one sheet, bearing the letterhead of Santé Prison in Paris. He scanned quickly down to the signature. It read: Arsène Lupin. Breathing rapidly, the baron read the letter.
My dearest Baron Cahorn:
Allow me to applaud you on your exquisite collection of fine art.
To the baron’s horror, not only did the letter name in detail the paintings and other treasures inside his castle, but the writer also revealed the exact location of each item he specifically wanted.
"How could anyone possibly know?" the baron shouted into the air. "No one has set foot inside my castle!" He continued to read.

I humbly request that these particular items be packed carefully and shipped to me, within eight days, to the address below. However, if you will not oblige, then I will have to remove them myself. Expect me on the night of September 27. I apologize for any inconvenience.
Sincerely,
Arsène Lupin
P.S. Don’t send the Jean-Antoine Watteau painting. Although you paid thirty thousand francs for it, it is only a copy.

The letter quite upset the baron. Being well acquainted with the recent crimes reported in the newspapers, he was only too familiar with the name Arsène Lupin. He knew Lupin had been arrested in America by the celebrated detective Ganimard and was now imprisoned in Santé Prison. The baron, however, also knew that with Lupin nothing was impossible.

That evening the baron wrote a letter to the local police captain, enclosing Lupin’s letter and requesting protection. The reply came immediately, informing the baron that Lupin was in Santé Prison under close surveillance and without letter-writing privileges. No doubt the letter was from an impostor making idle threats.
Still the baron was not convinced, and his hopelessness and despair grew as each day passed. However, one morning he found a glimmer of hope when he read the Caudebec Revealer , a local newspaper.

"‘The celebrated detective who captured Arsène Lupin has been spotted in town, taking a well-deserved rest. An enthusiastic fisherman, Detective Ganimard is seldom missing from the river,’" Baron Cahorn read aloud and then cried, "Ganimard is here! Only he can help!"
The town of Caudebec was just six kilometers away, so immediately the baron went to the offices of the Revealer and spoke to the reporter who had written the article.
"Ganimard?" the young reporter repeated.
"It is of the utmost urgency!" exclaimed the baron. "You must tell me where he is."

The reporter scratched his head and said, "You are sure to find him fishing on the riverbank. I happened to meet him there one day and noticed that his name was engraved on his fishing pole." He pointed outside his window at a man wearing a straw hat and fishing at the river’s edge. "There he is now."

The baron left the reporter and ran toward the river. He approached the famous Ganimard and introduced himself. The detective, however, responded with silence. Then the baron burst forth with his story about his treasures, Lupin, and the letter, as the man sat motionless.
"Please, Monsieur Ganimard," pleaded the baron, "I am in desperate need of your help."
Without removing his eyes from his fishing pole, the man replied, "Burglars do not customarily warn people before they rob them, especially Lupin."
"But the letter . . ."
"If this were the work of Lupin," said Ganimard with a slight smile, "which it obviously is not, it would be my pleasure to assist you, Baron. Unfortunately Lupin is already locked up."
"He could have escaped," the baron retorted.
Ganimard finally faced him, unsmiling.
"No one has ever escaped Santé Prison," said the detective. "Now, go home and sleep soundly—you’re frightening the fish." Then he turned his gaze back to the river.

The baron went home, somewhat reassured by Ganimard’s words. He was beginning to believe that he had possibly overreacted, but every night he still checked each bolt and lock in the castle. When September 26 arrived, so did a message, and the baron’s initial anxieties were reawakened.
"A telegram for you, sir," announced a servant.
The baron snatched the telegram and read: The items I requested have not been delivered. Prepare to see me tomorrow night. Lupin
The baron hastened to Caudebec and found Ganimard at the same spot by the river.
"Lupin is coming!" the baron shouted as he shoved the telegram in the detective’s face. "Now he will take away my treasures!"
Ganimard put down his fishing pole and said in a cold voice, "I’m on vacation. I don’t want to bother myself with such silliness."
"Come to my castle and protect my valuables," the baron begged. "Name your price."
Ganimard smiled coolly and said, "You will be throwing your money out the window."
"I don’t care," cried the baron.
"Then I accept on one condition," replied Ganimard. "You must not speak to anyone of my involvement. It must be kept a secret."
"You have my word," the baron promised.
"I’ll see you tomorrow evening at nine o’clock, and I’ll be bringing some men to help me," said the detective. "Before I arrive, put all your valuables in one room in the main part of the castle."

The next day, September 27, Baron Cahorn put all his valuables into one room in the main part of the castle as he had been instructed. Pacing like a guard in front of the building, he saw nothing and heard nothing. At eight thirty the baron dismissed his servants, and at nine o’clock Ganimard appeared with two huge men.
The baron took the men into the room where all his treasures had been placed with obvious care. Ganimard inspected the door, windows, and walls━they were closed and barricaded.
"Give me the key to this room, Baron," he commanded. "I will lock my men inside." Turning to the men, he continued, "At the slightest sound, call me." The men nodded once in unison.
The baron and Ganimard positioned themselves in a small room that used to be the watchman’s quarters. From there they had a clear view of the bridge and the entrance to the old tunnel.
"Is this tunnel closed up?" asked Ganimard.
"Yes."
"Then, unless there is another entrance known only to Lupin, we are quite safe."
Ganimard put three chairs together and stretched himself upon them. "I feel guilty taking your money, Baron," he said, laughing. "Soon you will see this was nothing but a joke."

But the baron was not laughing, and he waited anxiously. He heard the clock strike eleven, twelve, and one. The only other sounds Baron Cahorn could hear were the loud snores of Ganimard. Finally, at dawn, the baron aroused the detective from his slumber.
"Nothing has happened!" the baron cried joyfully.
Yawning, Ganimard replied, "What did I tell you?"
They went and unlocked the room containing the baron’s possessions.
"My pictures! My furniture! All carried away!" screamed the baron, falling to his knees and weeping.
The room had been emptied, except for Ganimard’s sleeping men.
Ganimard looked around the room. "Window and door locks are intact. No breaks in the walls or ceiling."
The detective shook his men violently━no response. Then he noticed two empty glasses on the floor. "They’ve been drugged," he said.
"By Lupin, right? It was Lupin," the baron whispered.
Ganimard could only nod.
"Are there any clues?" wailed the baron.
"It is Arsène Lupin. He leaves no clues. He makes no mistakes!" Ganimard retorted.
"I’ll call the police," replied the baron sadly.
"Remember your promise," said Ganimard. "You will tell no one about me."

And so the fortress of Baron Cahorn became the center of public attention, as the police swarmed through every room and the bridge became congested with curious onlookers. The newspapers published stories about the case, and reporters even obtained the letter Arsène Lupin had sent to the baron. No one knew how they obtained that letter, but it caused a lot of excitement. Everyone was wondering, how did the thieves get into the castle?
A few weeks later, the local police asked for help from the Paris police, who decided to send their best detective: Ganimard.
The famous detective listened quietly as Monsieur Dudouis, the Paris police chief, filled him in on the case.
"In my opinion the solution to this problem lies with Arsène Lupin," Ganimard said to his superior.
"That is absurd," said Dudouis. "Lupin is in prison."
"Lupin is the only man in France," declared Ganimard, "who has the imagination and sufficient resources to carry out such a bold scheme."
So Ganimard was given permission to interview Lupin in Santé Prison.
"Dear Ganimard, how delightful to see you!" cried Lupin, welcoming the detective like an old friend. "Sorry I cannot offer you any refreshments." Lupin gestured to his cramped, bare cell.
"The only thing I want from you is answers," Ganimard replied gruffly.
"Anything, just ask," Lupin said sweetly. "Although I must admit that I already know about the Cahorn affair." Arsène Lupin then described the items stolen from the castle one by one.
"Was it all your work?" Ganimard asked when he had finished.
"Naturally," Lupin replied.
"How did you carry it out?" said Ganimard.
"I don’t usually divulge my methods, but I will share with you a theory from which you may deduce your own conclusions," answered Lupin, smiling graciously.
"Proceed," Ganimard growled.

"Let us suppose that a wealthy man, we will call him Cahorn for the sake of convenience, receives a letter warning him that the notorious Lupin is going to rob him. The police do not take him seriously. Then one day he reads in the paper of a celebrated detective in town. What would he do?"
"Seek out the detective," Ganimard replied. "But how did the newspaper know the detective would be there?"
"Quite simple," Lupin said. "Suppose Lupin had asked one of his friends to tell a reporter about the detective’s holiday plans?"
"I see," said Ganimard. "Plant a fake story."

"And a fake detective too." Lupin smiled. "Of course, to appear authentic, the fake detective refuses to help Cahorn. And then the telegram arrives, and Cahorn rushes back to the detective to offer him money to help."
"Ah," Ganimard replied, "the victim invites the thief to his home . . ."
"Where he has obediently gathered all his treasures into one room," Lupin continued.
"How did he remove the items?" asked Ganimard. "Cahorn never slept a wink."

"The two assistants lowered them down with rope onto a boat rented especially for the occasion," explained Lupin. "The baron did not hear anything that night because of the unusually loud snoring of the fake detective. Plus the snores served another purpose." Lupin was grinning now. "As long as the detective snored, his two assistants knew it was safe to proceed. Then they took mild drugs to knock themselves unconscious."
"Simple yet ingenious," marveled Ganimard. "But who was the famous detective on a fishing trip?"
"There could be only one," Lupin said, his eyes dancing.
Ganimard’s jaw dropped. "Are you saying . . .?"
"The world’s most celebrated detective━Ganimard, who captured Arsène Lupin!" proclaimed Lupin dramatically.
Ganimard stared in astonishment for a long time. Then he burst out laughing.
"Yes, Ganimard must arrest Ganimard as an accomplice!" said Lupin.
Just then a prison guard brought Lupin his lunch, which was furnished by a neighboring restaurant, and then left the cell.

"But don’t worry, my friend, the Cahorn affair is just about to be settled," said Lupin, biting into some bread. "You will learn that the fake Ganimard is still on very good terms with the baron, and the baron has authorized him to negotiate a sum with me to recover his treasures. Then the baron will withdraw his complaint. So there is no theft!"
"How do you know all that?" asked Ganimard.

"I have just received the telegram I was expecting," said Lupin, breaking an egg from his lunch tray. The shell contained a small piece of paper that read: Contract closed. One hundred thousand francs delivered.
"You won’t think you’re so smart at your trial," said Ganimard.
"Forgive me, but I have decided not to attend my trial."
Ganimard glared at the prisoner, speechless, and then turned to leave.
"Oh, you have forgotten your watch," said Lupin. "Somehow it strayed into my pocket."
Ganimard patted the empty pocket where his watch was usually kept.
Lupin smiled, his eyes twinkling as he whistled an aria from The Magic Flute .

Arsène Lupin had just finished eating and was feeling very pleased with himself. He took an expensive cigar from his pocket and started to examine it carefully. Just as he was about to remove the gold band around the cigar, his cell door opened. Lupin deftly tossed the cigar into a drawer while he moved forward to welcome his visitor with a warm smile.
"I am ready for my daily exercise, dear boy," Lupin said to a guard waiting by the cell door.
After the guard had led Lupin outside, two men entered the prisoner’s cell. One man was Inspector Dieuzy; the other was Inspector Folenfant.
"What are we searching for again?" asked Dieuzy.

"Any evidence that Lupin has been communicating with someone outside the prison," replied Folenfant. On the previous evening, a well-known Paris newspaper had published these words addressed to the reporter covering Lupin’s court case:
Monsieur:
Your recent news story depicted me in a most unfavorable way. A few days before my trial, I will make you sorry for what you wrote.
Arsène Lupin
Clearly the letter had been written and signed by Arsène Lupin. Yet prisoners at the Santé Prison were forbidden to have contact with the outside, even through letters.

"It’s obvious Lupin is arrogantly announcing that he plans to escape━and in the newspaper!" Monsieur Dudouis, the chief of the Paris police, had shouted. "This does not reflect well on the prison." He pointed to the two inspectors. "Tomorrow you will search his cell."
So Dieuzy and Folenfant were now checking the bed linens, the cracks in the walls and the ceiling, and even the toilet. They were about to give up when Dudouis appeared.
"Well?" said the police chief, quietly making his presence known.
"We found nothing, sir," answered Dieuzy.
"Wait a minute," said Folenfant suddenly. "I remember Lupin shutting that drawer just before the guard led him outside."
"Well, let’s see," said Dudouis, opening the drawer. He pulled out a stack of newspaper clippings that all related to Lupin. Some text was underlined and a few words were circled.
"Perhaps this is some secret code," mused Dudouis. "Anything else?"
"Just this cigar, sir," replied Folenfant, picking it up and handing it over to his superior.
"Where did he get this?" demanded Dudouis.
"It must have come with his breakfast, sir," said Folenfant.

"Our friend Lupin has excellent taste," noted Dudouis, examining the gold band. Then he gently squeezed the cigar next to his ear to test its quality. "A good cigar should crackle a bit," he explained. But the cigar was flexible and made no sound. Upon further inspection the police chief noticed something white between the tobacco leaves. Delicately, with the aid of a toothpick he took from his pocket, Dudouis carefully removed a piece of very thin paper. He unrolled it and read: The basket has taken the place of the others. Eight out of ten are ready now. Press the outer foot on the plate and push downward. From 12 to 16 every day, H-P will wait. But where? Reply immediately. Don’t worry; your friend is here.
Dudouis pondered the cryptic words. "Basket? I think I know what that means, and ‘12 to 16’ must mean from noon until four o’clock," he said.
"A very astute observation, sir," said Folenfant.
"Lupin is definitely making plans to escape, sir," said Dieuzy. "But who or what is H-P?"
"I don’t know," Dudouis replied and then added, "Apparently the prisoner has not read this message yet, as we can tell from the condition of the cigar."
"How did he get this message?" asked Dieuzy.
"They must come hidden in his meals," explained Dudouis. "This must be the way he communicates with whoever is helping him from outside."

The police chief replaced the cigar with one of his own and carefully hid the note in it. "We will wait to see how Lupin replies," he said with a sharp glint in his eye. Then the three men left the cell.
That evening Lupin finished his meal and a guard retrieved his tray. Just outside the cell, however, Folenfant intercepted it and took it to Dudouis.
"Check everything," the police chief ordered. "Lupin’s reply will be here somewhere."

They examined the dishes, the tray, and the utensils. Suddenly Dudouis let out a cry of joy. Inside the wooden handle of the knife was a piece of paper. It read simply: Make sure that H-P follows at a distance every day. I will go ahead. Thank you, dear friend.
"At last!" cried Monsieur Dudouis gleefully. "We have him! A little strategy on our part, and we will catch not only Arsène Lupin, but his associates as well."
The police chief grabbed Folenfant’s hands, and they danced around the room.

For several months Arsène Lupin had been transported weekly to appear before Judge Bouvier, who was overseeing his case. One day the famous prisoner ignored his own lawyer and comically confessed to every charge against him: burglaries in a dozen neighborhoods, counterfeiting, and a bank robbery. "I confess I did everything, and there is ten times as much that you know nothing about," said Lupin.

Frustrated by Lupin’s arrogance, the judge refused to see the thief again until he agreed to get serious about his upcoming trial. But when Dudouis showed the judge Lupin’s secret messages, Bouvier exploded in anger.
"Bring that man back into my court!" the judge roared. "Monsieur Dudouis, I solemnly order you to do whatever is necessary to prevent his escape!"
"As you wish, Judge," said Dudouis.
"Starting tomorrow," continued Bouvier, "I want to see Lupin every day until he tells me what I want to know." The two men shook hands.

So Lupin was taken to the judge every day with the other prisoners. All prisoners going to the courthouse were transported in the morning in horse-drawn police vans. These vans were nicknamed salad baskets because each van was divided into ten small cells, or baskets, five on each side. These cells, one for every prisoner, were constructed with iron bars, and riding in them was very uncomfortable. The prisoners usually left the courthouse after lunch and returned to Santé Prison between three and four, but one afternoon a decision was made to take Arsène Lupin back to the prison alone since the other prisoners had been delayed in court.
"Choose any seat you like," said the guard to Lupin, laughing. Then the guard shut the door and climbed up into the driver’s seat.
Once inside the van, Lupin moved to the third cell on his right and sat down. Soon the van began to move.

"Where is that plate?" Lupin whispered to himself. He searched the floor with his right foot. "Ah, here it is. Now I press down on it . . ." The plate opened to reveal the street going by and two of the van’s wheels. Suddenly the van stopped. Loud, angry voices erupted from outside━a sick horse was blocking traffic, including another police van. Lupin took that moment to squeeze out of the hole in the bottom of the van and leap to the ground. He was free!

Looking around, Lupin saw that two wagons had collided and angry drivers were about to come to blows. A block away a coachman saw Lupin drop out of the prison van and start to run. The coachman tried to alert the guard, but his voice was drowned out by the street noise.
Lupin turned back, waved, and then saluted before disappearing into the crowd.

After escaping from the police van, Arsène Lupin had run for a few steps, but once he was on the sidewalk, he walked leisurely, like a casual stroller in the city. He whistled happily, greeted other pedestrians with nods, and headed to a nearby sidewalk cafe. The beautiful autumn day attracted many to these outdoor restaurants, but Lupin found a seat right away and ordered a glass of the most expensive wine. When his glass was almost empty, Lupin called for the cafe owner.
"Yes, monsieur, what can I do for you?" the owner asked when he arrived at Lupin’s table.
In a voice loud enough for all to hear, Lupin said, "I regret to say that I have forgotten my wallet. Perhaps, because my name is very recognizable, you will accept an IOU. My name is Arsène Lupin."
The owner thought he was joking.

"I am Lupin, once a prisoner at Santé Prison but now a fugitive," said Lupin emphatically. "I’m sure my name inspires your complete confidence in me." Then he got up and walked away as the other diners burst into laughter and the owner stood there amazed.

Later that afternoon Monsieur Dudouis, chief of the Paris police, stood staring blankly at the awards on an office wall at Santé Prison. "Those awards won’t mean anything if Lupin is not found," he thought.

Dudouis had come to the prison to investigate how Arsène Lupin had accomplished the impossible when a miracle happened. A guard burst into the office, shouting, "He has returned! Lupin has turned himself in!"
Dudouis shoved the guard aside and ran outside to see Lupin being escorted by two other guards. Lupin smiled when he saw Dudouis.
"I suppose it’s pointless to ask you how and why?" said the police chief through clenched teeth.
"I did it because I could do it," Lupin retorted with a sly smile.

"I will not be mocked!" cried Dudouis angrily. "Go explain yourself to Judge Bouvier!" The chief then ordered Lupin to be taken to the judge immediately. After Lupin had left, Dudouis thought, "Perhaps the public does not know of Lupin’s escape and we can avoid any embarrassment."

But, at that precise moment, Paris was hungrily devouring a special edition of the newspaper Echo de France . This newspaper seemed to concentrate exclusively on the exploits of Arsène Lupin. In this edition the Echo printed every detail of Lupin’s escape, including the messages exchanged between the prisoner and his mysterious friend, the incident at the outdoor cafe, and even the fact that the police and the judge knew of the escape plans beforehand. The information had been submitted to the Echo by an anonymous writer, and everything had been disclosed!
While everyone was reading about the escape, Lupin was giving a firsthand account of his escape to Judge Bouvier. But rather than being impressed, the judge laughed scornfully.
"Why are you laughing?" Lupin demanded. He was annoyed that the judge didn’t seem to know that even the great detective Ganimard had applauded Lupin’s intelligence.
The judge wiped tears from his bulging eyes. "You are an impudent and egotistical maniac."
Lupin’s eyes flashed angrily for a second, but he quickly calmed himself. "I promise, Judge, that this escape was but a preliminary to something grander. My great escape will take place shortly."
"Well, don’t forget you have a trial coming up," said the judge sarcastically.
"Perhaps I did not make myself clear," Lupin said, staring directly into the judge’s eyes. "I will not be present at my trial."
"Oh, you won’t?" sneered the judge.
"Nothing can change my mind now," declared Lupin. "It has been decided."

Lupin’s confidence, combined with the inexplicable crimes that he had committed, annoyed and mystified the officers of the law. Only Lupin knew why he did such things, and he revealed his secrets only when he wanted to.

Upon returning to Santé Prison, Lupin was transferred to another cell and two new guards were posted to watch his every move. The judge closed the investigation and no further action was taken for two months. Lupin did not raise any objections, and after his return, he seemed cheerless and subdued, spending most of his time lying on his cot with his face to the wall. He hardly spoke and rarely even ate. He seemed to have lost his zest for life.

Public curiosity had only become stronger as the date of Lupin’s trial neared, and everyone thought the infamous prisoner would indeed escape again. People anticipated a lively trial bubbling with Lupin’s charisma and genius. On the opening day of the trial, enormous crowds gathered on benches in the courtroom, anxious to see the dashing gentleman burglar. But the prisoner who walked in was a complete contrast to what the public expected. He walked in slowly with his head bent down, long hair covering his face, and his clothes hanging loosely on his thin body. Then he sat down solemnly next to his lawyer.
"The prisoner will rise and state his name," said the court clerk.
The prisoner rose but said nothing.
"Your name?" Judge Bouvier repeated.
In a slow and deep voice, the prisoner replied, "Baudru, Désiré."
A confused murmur spread through the courtroom. The judge burst out laughing.
"Baudru? Is that your new alias? Fine. Then I shall state your name for the record: Arsène Lupin."
The courtroom buzzed with excitement.

Bouvier banged his gavel and continued, "As for your real name and identity, that is a mystery. You appeared in our city three years ago, and we believe you were a man called Rostat, who worked alongside the great magician Hugo. We also believe you were a Russian student named Vladimir, who worked with the famed bacteriologist Dr. Altier. You were the professor who introduced Japanese martial arts to the people of Paris, the cyclist who won the Grand Prix━who, after receiving his prize, was never seen again━and the person who saved many people from a deadly fire while picking their pockets. We have evidence that all these people are one and the same━Arsène Lupin."
The people in the courtroom whispered to each other.
"As you see, you are not as clever as you think," said the judge. "This, I’m afraid, is the end of your journey."
The prisoner remained silent, his shoulders drooping, and he shifted from one foot to the other.
Detective Ganimard was in the courtroom too, and he observed the actions of the prisoner closely. "This doesn’t look like the man I arrested," he thought.
The judge read the various charges against Lupin and then demanded, "Do you confess that you are Arsène Lupin and that you committed these crimes?"

The prisoner lifted his head, revealing his hollow cheeks and sunken eyes. The crowd leaned forward, and many thought that this man couldn’t be the vibrant, youthful man with twinkling eyes so often described in the newspapers.
The prisoner spoke. "No. My name is Baudru."

The entire courtroom erupted in laughter, except for Detective Ganimard, and as the trial proceeded, he continued to scrutinize the prisoner. He felt uneasy and deeply suspicious, and before he was called to testify, he interrupted the trial.
"Your Honor? I seek permission to speak," said Ganimard boldly.
"What is it?" asked Bouvier.
Ganimard pointed to the prisoner and declared in a strong voice: "The man before you is not Arsène Lupin!"
Detective Ganimard repeated his declaration. "This man is not Arsène Lupin! Somehow Lupin has put this poor devil in his place."
The courtroom erupted in astonished cries, and not even Judge Bouvier could bring order. The prisoner was taken away while the court adjourned until further notice.
The judge interviewed the men who had guarded Lupin in his cell.
"Who is the prisoner?" demanded the judge.
"Arsène Lupin?" said one guard hesitantly.
"Uh, at least we think he was . . . ," added the other.
"You think ?" Bouvier’s nostrils flared wildly. "You have spent the past two months with this man! Is he or isn’t he Lupin?"
"Well, he was so quiet," confessed the first guard. "He spent most of the time lying on his cot, facing the wall."
Finally the guards admitted they could not swear the prisoner was Arsène Lupin.
Next Judge Bouvier sent for Monsieur Dudouis.
"Was that Lupin or not?" the judge asked the shaken police chief.
"I do not know," he replied truthfully. Dudouis had not recognized the prisoner in the courtroom.
Judge Bouvier sighed. "Then explain how this man was substituted for Lupin."
"I cannot," replied Dudouis in a defeated voice.
The judge called the court into session once more, banged his gavel for order, and had the prisoner brought in. Ganimard took his seat again in the courtroom.
"Monsieur Baudru, how and when did you come to be at Santé Prison?" the judge gently asked the prisoner. He did not wish to frighten the man.

Baudru seemed to relax. "Two months ago I was homeless and sleeping on the street," he replied in a weary voice. "The police put me in a cell at the courthouse overnight. A judge gave me a warning, and I was released the next day."
"Then what happened?" asked Bouvier.
"Well, I was standing outside the courthouse when suddenly I was grabbed by two guards."
"And?" the judge prompted.
Baudru shrugged. "They put me into a prison van and took me to Santé Prison. Since then I’ve been in cell 24."
"Lupin’s cell," muttered Bouvier.
Baudru shrugged again and said, "Truth be told, Judge, I was happy in cell 24. I got food, a warm bed, and hot showers."
At Baudru’s response the courtroom burst into laughter.
The prisoner was returned to cell 24 until his case could be investigated more thoroughly, and later that evening, Judge Bouvier, Dudouis, and Ganimard met privately.
"We have discovered that the precise day and time Baudru was outside the courthouse corresponds to the moment Lupin left court for Santé Prison in a prison van," began Dudouis.
"Could the guards have made a mistake?" said the detective. "Perhaps they mistook Baudru for Lupin?"
"Or is Baudru an accomplice?" asked the judge.

"You have no grounds to hold Baudru," said Ganimard. "You must release him. But my men and I will keep him under close surveillance. If he is working with Lupin, sooner or later he will lead us to him."
The men agreed on this arrangement, and Monsieur Dudouis appointed Inspectors Folenfant and Dieuzy to assist Ganimard in watching Baudru.

A few days later, Désiré Baudru was released from Santé Prison, and the first thing he did was enter a secondhand-clothing store. He exchanged his tattered jacket and vest for an old but wearable coat and walked to the bus depot. The bus he wanted to take was full, so Baudru sat in the waiting room.
Just outside the depot, Ganimard gave instructions to his two assistants. "Men, go and stop a carriage for us. When Baudru gets on the next bus, we’ll follow him."
The two men obeyed. Then Ganimard entered the waiting room, but it was empty.
"I’m an idiot!" cried Ganimard. "I forgot there was another exit."

Ganimard rushed through the rear exit just in time to catch sight of Baudru getting onto another bus. With no time to give instructions to his assistants, Ganimard had to follow Baudru on his own. He ran and pulled himself up onto the bus as it left the depot.

"There he is," observed Ganimard. Baudru was already fast asleep on a seat. His mouth was half open, his head was rolling from side to side, and there was an incredible expression of stupidity on his smudged face. "This man must be who he says he is," said Ganimard to himself. "He’s certainly incapable of deceiving anyone."
Suddenly Baudru stood up. He got off at the next stop and started walking leisurely toward a nearby park. He was whistling as if he were in a good mood.
"Ah, he’s glad he’s a free man," Ganimard thought as he followed close behind.

After an hour Baudru finally sat down on a park bench, and Ganimard continued to watch him from behind a tree. But after thirty minutes, the detective could stand it no longer. He approached Baudru and sat down next to him.
"It’s a beautiful day," Ganimard said cheerfully.

No response. Then the man threw his head back and laughed merrily. The hairs on Ganimard’s neck stood up. "I know that laugh!" he thought. Ganimard swiftly grabbed the man by his collar and looked hard into his face. The twinkling eyes staring back at him were undeniably Lupin’s.
"Arsène Lupin!" he stammered, tightening his hold.
Suddenly Lupin made a slight movement and a surge of pain went up Ganimard’s arm. The detective quickly released his hold.

"If you had taken my martial arts class you would know that with a little more pressure, I could have broken your arm," Lupin said calmly, straightening his collar. "And you would have deserved it. I am surprised that you, an old friend, should treat me in such an abusive way."
Ganimard stood there stunned for a moment and then said, "I can’t believe it was my testimony that allowed Baudru, I mean you, to be released."
"My dear Ganimard, do not take it personally. If it hadn’t been you, I would have arranged for someone else to testify," Lupin said lightly.
"But how did you change your appearance?" whispered Ganimard.

"As the judge kindly mentioned, working alongside Dr. Altier, the bacteriologist, I learned which substances can change skin color and texture. Hugo, the magician, taught me how to hold my muscles and body a certain way. Add to that two months of dieting in cell 24, and voilà!" Lupin stood and spread his arms. "The trick is complete!"
"And Baudru?" asked Ganimard.
"Oh, he is real—a poor, harmless fellow. Baudru and I share many similar features, so my friends arranged for him to be outside the courthouse about the same time I was there."
"But there was no substitution," said Ganimard.

"It was me all along, my good man," said Lupin. "An actual substitution would have been too difficult. So I created the public belief that Arsène Lupin would escape and would not be present at the trial."
"And we believed it too," said Ganimard. "The judge, the police . . ."

"During the trial I admit I had a small worry that I would be recognized. But you, my reliable friend, spoke with such conviction—‘This man is not Arsène Lupin!’ Everyone was prepared to believe you." Lupin clapped his hands.
Ganimard hung his head. "What do you plan to do now?"
"Well, I will shower, rest, and change into something more presentable. Tonight I have a most important engagement," Lupin said, turning to leave.
"What is it?" asked Ganimard.
"Tonight I dine with the British ambassador!" Lupin walked away and disappeared among the trees.

My friends had invited me to stay at their château on the banks of the Seine. First, I would travel by rail to the Rouen station, where my automobile would be waiting for me. Then I would drive the remaining distance.

I boarded the train in Paris, but the passengers in my compartment were smoking, an awful habit. So I took my overcoat, newspaper, and timetable and sought refuge in a neighboring compartment. It was occupied by a woman who scrutinized me suspiciously as I entered. I smiled and had just settled into my seat when the door suddenly opened and a man rushed in. The woman let out a small cry and clenched her handkerchief. The man was dressed elegantly; I noticed his stylish silk shirt and leather gloves. He was young and handsome, and there was something vaguely familiar about his face.
The whistle sounded as the train pulled out of the station, and I turned to look at the woman.
"Are you ill, madame?" I asked, because her face was devoid of all color.

Her frightened eyes met mine. "Monsieur . . . ," she whispered in a trembling voice, "that man . . ." She nodded slightly toward the newcomer, who had settled on a seat and appeared to be sleeping. "Do you recognize him?"
"No. Why do you ask?" I whispered back.
She leaned toward me. "He is Arsène Lupin."
I looked at the sleeping gentleman again; he seemed perfectly harmless.
"Madame, that isn’t plausible," I assured her. "Just yesterday, a large reward was announced for Lupin’s capture. Surely, he would not be so imprudent as to make a public appearance the day after."
The woman’s voice grew a bit louder. "My husband is a director with the prison system. He received word that police were searching for Arsène Lupin at the Paris train station."
"Yet he allowed you to board this train?"
"Lupin was said to be traveling to Nice," she replied less confidently. "But he must have switched trains."
"Madame, don’t be afraid," I said. "Even if Lupin is aboard this train, the last thing he wants to do is draw attention to himself."

My words did not reassure her, and she turned her face to the window. I opened my newspaper and read reports of Lupin’s trial, but I soon lost interest. I drifted into a deep slumber and dreamed of Arsène Lupin as a menacing black shape coming toward me, growing larger and larger. With a cry, I awoke to find our traveling companion had leaped on top of me and now had his knee on my chest. One hand was around my throat, and the other was rummaging through my pockets for my wallet.

"Keep still and I won’t hurt you," he said as I started to choke. He took a rope out of his pocket and quickly tied me up. The man turned to the woman. "Madame, give me your handkerchief," he commanded in a calm but threatening voice. He stuffed the handkerchief into my mouth, and within moments, I was bound, gagged, and helpless.

The man was cool, deft, and audacious: traits possessed by the gentleman burglar himself—Arsène Lupin! But he was not Arsène Lupin, because Lupin was the man lying on the floor, gagged and bound. Yes, I was the helpless victim!
"Give me your purse," the thief said to the frightened woman.
"My jewels are in there," she sobbed as she reluctantly handed him her purse.
"Take off your rings too," he ordered.
Trembling with fear, she pulled the rings from her fingers and handed them to the thief. Then she fainted. He put her rings and my wallet into the purse.

I thought: "Here I am, Arsène Lupin, robbed like an unsophisticated novice." As I lay there, I pondered the various problems this situation presented. First, that man now had my wallet. The money was not important, but the wallet held papers containing information—the names of my associates, plans, addresses, and other documents—that could lead to my capture. I was going to visit friends who knew me by the name Guillaume Berlat, and my likeness to Lupin was always a source of jokes to them, so I wore no disguise. I knew the Rouen police would question me, but I had a fake identity card in my wallet saying I was a deputy police officer. However, now I was no longer free, had no identity card, and could not use any of my usual tricks. Plus, the woman would scream the minute someone opened the compartment door once the train stopped. "What am I going to do?" I thought.
"Ah, just what I need," the man said as he scanned my timetable. He found what he was looking for, strode to the window, and looked out.
"Surely, he is not going to jump," I thought. The train was moving at an alarming speed, but then it slowed down as it entered a tunnel.

"Oh, it’s raining," muttered the man, and he took the woman’s umbrella and put on my overcoat. Then he left our compartment, and just as the train slowed almost to a halt, he jumped out the door of the train.
"He stole my jewels!" screamed the woman as the train started to speed up again. The distraught woman was weeping over her lost possessions without a care for me lying there.
I gave her an imploring look and she quickly removed my gag.
"I’ll untie you too," she said.
"No, the police must see everything as it is," I replied.
"Monsieur," she cried, "didn’t I say he was on this train?"
"Don’t worry, the police will catch him."
"Catch Lupin? How?" she sniffed.

"Listen carefully, madame, and do as I tell you," I began. "When we arrive in Rouen, the police will come and you must tell them everything that happened. Give a description . . . his silk shirt, facial features, your umbrella, his gray overcoat—"
"Your coat," she interjected.
"No, you are mistaken," I replied hastily.
"I don’t think he had a coat," she said.
"It must be his, because it was not mine. Give your name and your husband’s position. That will make them search more zealously."
"And you?"

"I am Guillaume Berlat. If necessary, tell them you know me, that I’m a friend of your husband. That will save time and will accelerate the investigation. The important thing is capturing Arsène Lupin and recovering your jewels!" I insisted.
When the train arrived at Rouen station, an officer opened our compartment and the woman gave an account of what had occurred.
"Poor Monsieur Berlat, my husband’s dear friend, was brutally assaulted," she cried.
I was immensely proud of her performance.
"But what happened to Lupin?" asked the officer as he untied me.
"He jumped off the train," she continued. "He was wearing a silk shirt—"
"Like Monsieur Berlat’s?" asked the officer, glancing at me.
"Yes, and he had a gray overcoat . . ." She paused and glanced at me. I held my breath.
"We received a telegram saying Lupin wore a gray overcoat," said the police officer, nodding.

I was taken to the station physician, and after a brief examination, I was pronounced "shaken, but in strong spirits." Then I approached the Rouen police chief and his officers on the platform. In a weak voice, I said, "Sirs, this was indeed the work of Lupin. And if we hurry, I think I can help."
And that is how Arsène Lupin came to be searching for Arsène Lupin!
My plan to capture the thief, recover my papers, and then make my escape had to be thorough. I told the officers about "Lupin" consulting my timetable.

"Lupin leaped off the train in the tunnel, which is close by the Darnétal station," I explained. "He will probably take the train that goes to Amiens, since that is the next train. It leaves the station at 10:20"—I glanced at my watch—"exactly 22 minutes from now."
"Really, monsieur," said one officer, as they stared at me in amazement. "That is a marvelous deduction."

Perhaps I had been too clever. I didn’t want them to be suspicious, so I laughed and said, "Ah, nothing sharpens the mind like having one’s wallet stolen." Then I dared to proceed with my bold suggestions.
"My automobile is here at the station, and if you permit me the assistance of two of your men, we can intercept Lupin at Darnétal," I said, addressing the police chief.
The police chief hesitated, but at that precise moment, my companion came to my rescue.

"I beg you, listen to Monsieur Berlat," she implored, a fresh wave of tears rolling down her cheeks. Her intervention was decisive, no doubt because her husband was a man of importance. So the police chief assigned two officers, named Massol and Delivet, to accompany me.

We raced off in my automobile, but unfortunately, we arrived at Darnétal Station three minutes too late. However, after talking to the stationmaster, Massol found out that a man in a gray overcoat had indeed purchased a ticket for Amiens and boarded the departed train.
"The train is an express," said Delivet, "but the next stop is in a mere 19 minutes. If we do not reach that stop before Lupin, we can proceed to Amiens."
"How far is it to the next station?" I asked.
"It’s 23 kilometers," he replied.
"Hmm, 19 minutes . . ." I made mental calculations. "We will arrive ahead of him!"
We hopped in the automobile, and I pushed hard on the gas pedal. We flew; the wheels barely touched the ground.
"Turn right here!" shouted Delivet.

As we made the turn, we saw a column of black smoke. It was the train! I pressed harder on the gas and raced side by side against the black monster. We reached the station just as the train came to a halt at the platform. A few passengers exited the train, but the thief was not among them.
"He must have seen us!" I cried in frustration. "He probably leaped from the train as it pulled into the station!"
"Look! There he is!" Delivet pointed to a figure crossing the tracks.

I started in pursuit, followed by the two officers. But Massol proved to be an exceptional runner and quickly disappeared into a grove of trees the thief had just entered. Delivet and I finally reached Massol a few minutes later, and he motioned for us to be quiet.
"There’s an abandoned barn back there," Massol whispered, barely out of breath. "That’s where Lupin is. He hasn’t seen me."
Gasping, I motioned to Delivet. "Go get help. He may be armed and dangerous." Removing both officers from the area was imperative to my escape plan.
Delivet did as he was told and retreated to the station.
"Monsieur Berlat, you remain here," Massol whispered. "This is a matter for the police."
"I appreciate that," I replied. "However, I am the only one who can recognize the man. I am willing to risk my life to ensure Lupin is caught for good!"
Massol saluted my bravery and handed me a pistol. "Shoot once if you are in distress, and we will come to your rescue, sir."

Massol hid himself behind a tall tree while I cautiously approached the barn. The door was slightly open and I could hear sounds of movement from within. I entered quietly and quickly familiarized myself with the surroundings. His back was turned toward me. In two strides, I was upon him. He tried to fire a revolver that he held in his hand. But he had no time. I threw him to the ground in such a manner that his arms were pinned beneath him. Twisted and helpless, I held him down with my knee on his chest.

"Listen, my boy," I began. "I am Arsène Lupin. I will let you up if you hand me, slowly and carefully, my wallet with all items intact, and the woman’s jewels. In return, I will save you from the police and enlist you as one of my associates. Answer, yes or no."
"Yes," he replied quickly.
"Very good," I said as I freed him and we both stood up. "Your escape this morning displayed exceptional precision and courage. I admire that."
Suddenly, he pulled a large knife from his trousers and lunged at me.

"Fool!" I exclaimed as I easily sidestepped his attack and gave him a sharp blow to the neck. He fell, stunned. I recovered my wallet, all my papers, and the woman’s purse from the overcoat pocket. Curious, I also pulled out the thief’s wallet and found an envelope with his name on it: Pierre Onfrey. Now, I realized why his face had seemed familiar on the train. I had seen his picture in the newspaper; he was a wanted murderer who had cut the throats of a woman and her two daughters.

"I must hurry," I said to myself. I put some money into an envelope with a card bearing these words: From Arsène Lupin to his worthy assistants, Massol and Delivet, with gratitude. I placed the envelope where it would be easily noticed and then rummaged through the woman’s purse. She had a few choice pieces of jewelry, which I instinctively pocketed, and I left her a ring made of green glass and a diamond pendant which did not appeal to my tastes. "What is that saying?" I thought, smiling to myself. "‘You can take the lion out of the jungle, but you cannot take the jungle out of the lion.’ Or was it a tiger?"

I carefully placed the purse next to the letter as Pierre began to stir. I prayed that Delivet had followed my orders to alert the other officers at the station and that they were nearby. I took the pistol Massol had given me and shot once into the air. Then I swiftly left the barn through a back door.

As I ran away, I heard the voices of Delivet and Massol calling out for me. Smiling, I crossed through the forest and found my automobile just where I had left it, unguarded and ready to transport me away. Later that evening, I arrived back in Paris and telegraphed my friends that I would not be visiting after all.
The following morning, the Écho printed this sensational item:
Dramatic events transpired yesterday. Arsène Lupin initiated the arrest of
the vicious murderer Pierre Onfrey. Being a gentleman, Lupin also restored to
Madame Renaud her purse, which had been stolen by Onfrey, and he also gave
generous compensation to the two detectives who assisted him in making the
arrest.
Lupin related this to me over a shared bottle of wine. Regrettably, some particulars have been omitted because my friend would be most displeased if I were to disclose every detail of his dealings.

The colorful history of the piece of jewelry known as "the Queen’s Necklace" started with its creation for Madame Du Barry, the last mistress of King Louis XV. Later, this necklace was owned by a cardinal who intended to give it to Marie Antoinette, the queen of France, before her head was so brutally removed from her neck. After passing through many hands over the years, and with only a few of the original diamonds remaining, the necklace was bought and restored by Gaston de Dreux-Soubise, the nephew of the cardinal. Although the Dreux-Soubise family’s financial fortunes dwindled with each generation, the family continued to take pride in the ownership of such a magnificent necklace.

Nearly a century later, Count Dreux-Soubise was keeping the necklace in a safety-deposit box at the bank. He removed it only for special occasions. One night, the count took the necklace out for his wife to wear to a royal reception for the king of Denmark. Everyone who attended commented on how the beauty of the countess was enhanced by the sparkling jewels. Afterward, the count and countess returned home, tired but elated by the attention the necklace and, consequently, they too, had received.
"I hate to take it off," the countess said as she walked into their bedroom, touching the necklace around her neck.
"Ah, there will be other occasions for you to impress royalty," said the count.

The countess removed the necklace and handed it to her husband, who carefully placed it in a red leather case. The count opened the door of a large closet that had been specially constructed to house the necklace when it was in their possession. He placed the box on a high shelf amid hatboxes and stacks of linen, closed the door, and retired to bed.

The next morning, the count arose intending to return the necklace to the bank before breakfast. However, he was called to the stables about a sick horse and was detained longer than he had anticipated. Finally, he went to the closet to retrieve the necklace.
"Back so soon from the bank?" His wife was up and getting her hair done by her maid.
"No, I’ll be leaving shortly," he replied as he rummaged around in the closet. The count reappeared with a curious expression. "Did you move it, dearest?"
"Move what?" asked his wife with a puzzled smile. Then, understanding the situation, her face lost all color.
"The necklace," said the count, stunned. "It’s not here."
His wife, pins sticking oddly out of her hair, jumped up. "You must be mistaken . . ."
"No, I’m not mistaken," he cried, throwing boxes and linens out of the closet. "I put it here on this shelf."
They searched the entire closet, but the necklace was gone. Resigned, the count called the police, and Inspector Valorbe arrived promptly.
"Are you sure no one entered your bedroom last night?" asked Valorbe after examining the closet.
"I am absolutely certain," the count said emphatically. "Besides, our room was bolted from the inside. I had to unbolt it this morning for my wife’s maid."
"There is no other entrance into your closet?" inquired the inspector.
"No," replied the count.
"Windows?" Valorbe took a candle into the closet.
"Yes, one, but it is closed up," said the count, pointing to a small window. The lower half was covered by a narrow curtain.
"What is outside the window?" asked Valorbe.
"A small inner courtyard," the count answered.
"Is there a floor above this?"
"There are two floors—most of the servants live there," explained the count. "But there is an iron grate over the court between this floor and the one above. That’s why this closet is so dark."
Valorbe removed the curtain and saw that the window was fastened. No one could have entered that way.
"Did any of your servants know that you wore the necklace last night?" asked the inspector, turning to the countess.
"Certainly," she replied. "But no one knew it was hidden in the closet, except . . ."
"Who, madame?" asked Valorbe.
"Henriette," the countess said a little louder, looking at her husband.
"Who is she?" asked the inspector.

"We went to school together," began the countess. "Her family disowned her for marrying a working-class boy. After he died, she needed a place for her and her son." The countess’ chin lifted slightly in pride. "She is good with a needle, so I said she could live here and work for me."
Valorbe and the countess went to Henriette’s apartment, which was on the same floor. Henriette was sewing, and her six-year-old son, Raoul, was sitting next to her, reading.

"My God!" the inspector thought when he saw how Henriette and her son lived. The small, dark room was hardly larger than a broom closet, and an even smaller room served as a kitchen. The place was wretched.
"I can’t believe it!" Henriette cried upon hearing of the theft.
"Could a thief have passed through your rooms, madame?" asked Valorbe.

"That’s impossible," Henriette replied. "I never go out." The boy stared at Valorbe with eyes that resembled his mother’s. "And look," she added as she opened her kitchen window. "It is at least three meters to the ledge of that closet window."
"Who told you the thief might have entered through that window?" the inspector asked pointedly.
Henriette replied in a puzzled voice, "That’s the closet window, is it not? The necklace was in there."
"How did you know that?" Valorbe persisted.
"I have always known it was kept there the night after a party. The countess told me."
The woman’s face, though still young, bore unmistakable traces of sorrow. She drew her son toward her as if some danger threatened them, and the child kissed his mother’s hand tenderly.

All that week, the investigation continued. Inspector Valorbe questioned the servants, reexamined the bolt and the closet window, and explored every inch of the small courtyard. The bolt had not been tampered with, and the window could not have been opened or closed from the outside. It was determined that Henriette had left the house only four times in the last three years and that the countess treated her very harshly. The case was closed due to lack of evidence and because the presiding judge secretly believed the count and countess had sold the necklace due to their poor financial situation. Even though Henriette had not been charged in the theft, the countess fired her.

As their income continued to drop, the count and countess had to sell off many of their possessions. Creditors kept calling to ask them for money, which they did not have. They would have been totally ruined if they had not inherited money from relatives.
Some months after Henriette was fired, the countess received a strange letter from her former schoolmate:
Madame, I do not know how to thank you! It was you, wasn’t it?
Puzzled, the countess wrote back, asking Henriette what her letter meant.
I have received two banknotes worth one thousand francs each. If you didn’t send them, who did? No one else knows where I live.

The next year, Henriette received another letter containing two thousand francs, and a third and fourth. However, the value of the notes doubled in value for the fifth and sixth years. These last two letters were signed "Anquety" and "Péchard." The return addresses were false.
After six years, Henriette died, and the mystery remained unsolved.

More than two decades had passed since the mysterious disappearance of the Queen’s Necklace. Count de Dreux-Soubise and his wife had traveled widely, maintaining a moderate social standing by inheriting from distant relatives. But one day, the couple decided to return to Paris and hold a dinner party at their old estate. Among the invited guests were the count’s nieces, a cousin, the mayor of Le Vésinet, an Italian military officer named Floriani whom the count had met in Sicily, and General Marquis de Rouzières, an old friend.

After the meal, coffee was served, and as was usual in the presence of the count and countess, the conversation turned toward the missing necklace. Each guest had a theory of how the theft had been carried out.
"Monsieur Floriani," said the countess, "what is your opinion?"
"Oh madame, I have none," Floriani replied graciously.
"Nonsense! Surely, you have a theory," insisted the general.

Floriani cleared his throat awkwardly. "I must admit, I have sometimes unraveled mysteries that have baffled even the greatest of detectives, though I am no Sherlock Holmes." He chuckled. "But I’m unfamiliar with the affair of the Queen’s Necklace."
Everyone then turned to the count, who told the story.
Floriani listened carefully, asked a few questions, and then said, "It is indeed a strange case, yet quite simple—"
"Simple?" barked the general. "This case left Paris’ cleverest police clueless!"

"It is simple because we are faced with one fact. The thief could only have entered by the bedroom door or the closet window," said Floriani mildly. "A person cannot open a bolted door from the outside. Therefore, the thief must have entered through the window."
The count shook his head. "The window was closed and fastened."
Floriani ignored the count’s remark and continued.
"To enter through the window, the thief simply had to construct some kind of bridge between Henriette’s kitchen window and the closet window ledge."
"But the window was fastened," repeated the count.
"Possibly, but did the window have a small, hinged opening at the top, a transom?" asked Floriani.
"How did you know that?" the count said.
"Many older houses have transom windows, and without a transom, the theft cannot be explained."
"But the transom was closed, like the window." The count frowned.
"No, it wasn’t," said Floriani. "If you had looked closely, you would have seen that it had been opened."
"How?" asked the count.
"Most transoms open by means of a wire with a ring at the end, no?" Floriani said.
The count nodded.
"Through a hole in the window, a person could pull the wire down using, for example, a poker hooked at the end, and open the transom," continued Floriani.
The count laughed. "Excellent! Your theory is very creative. But there was no hole in the window."
Floriani said quite seriously, "Yes, there was."
"Nonsense, we would have seen it," argued the count.
"Only if you were looking for it," Floriani replied. "I am certain there is a hole in the putty in the side of the window."
The guests began murmuring among themselves as the count wiped perspiration from his forehead.
"How can you, without even seeing where the theft took place, make such a statement?" the count demanded. "You are contradicting everything we know about this case."
Floriani shrugged. "It is only my theory. If I am wrong, you can easily prove it."
"I will do so at once," said the count and abruptly left the room.
Not a single word was said until the count returned to his guests.
"My love, what did you find?" the countess eagerly asked her husband.
The count merely shook his head in disbelief.
"What is it, man?" The general shook his friend’s arm.
The count took a deep breath. "There is a hole on the side of the window, just as Floriani said."
All eyes turned to Floriani.
"Please tell us the rest of your theory," implored the count.

Floriani took a sip of his drink and calmly went on. "I think the thief knew the countess was going to wear the necklace that evening. He prepared his bridge ahead of time, perhaps using some boards from a kitchen shelf. He waited until you retired, and then he crawled across the wooden bridge, pushed the poker through the putty, and pulled the transom ring."
"But the window lock was too far down to reach. How could he have opened the window?" asked the countess.
Floriani paused, and then said, "He must have crawled in through the transom."
"Impossible!" exclaimed the count. "It’s too small. No man could fit through such an opening."
"Then the thief must have been a child," Floriani declared.
The countess gasped, and her hand flew to her heart.
"Henriette had a son . . . Raoul," the count recalled.
"Henriette must have forced her son to do it!" cried the countess.
Floriani shook his head. "No, she had nothing to do with it."
"But how could she not know?" retorted the countess.

"It must have happened during the night, while she was sleeping. Moreover, you said Henriette thanked you for the banknotes she had received." Floriani paused; his voice became chilly. "Would she have done that if she were an accomplice to this theft?"
The guests shook their heads.
"Of course not," Floriani asserted. "But the child could have gone to a dealer, sold a diamond every year, and arranged for the money to be sent to his mother."
"And after Henriette died," said the countess, "what happened to the necklace?"
"Oh, I expect the boy kept it as a memento." Floriani smiled.
"Congratulations on your vivid imagination!" the count said, attempting to lighten the mood.
"I imagine nothing," Floriani replied. "I only explain events as they must have occurred."
"But what can you know of these events?" whispered the countess.

Floriani turned to her coolly. "From what you have told me, I have a good idea of what kind of life the mother and son had here. I can understand how the conditions they lived under and how they were treated could affect a young boy. He saw his mother suffer through the theft accusations, her illness, and consequently, her death. Years roll on. The boy became a man who desired very much to meet the people who had treated his mother so badly."
Floriani’s tone and manner had changed dramatically. Tension permeated the room.
"Who are you, monsieur?" the count asked suspiciously.

"I am Floriani, a man you met in Sicily. I only attempted to depict what Henriette’s son might have felt. The boy did what he did because he could not stand to see his mother suffer any longer." His voice cracked with emotion.

No one doubted now that Floriani was Henriette’s son, but what could the count and countess do about it? Who would believe that one of the greatest unsolved mysteries of all time was committed by an angry child?

The count tried to recapture the earlier lighthearted mood of the evening. "Your story is most entertaining," he said. "But I wonder what has become of Raoul? I hope he has not abandoned his career as a thief after such a dazzling debut."
Floriani’s eyes twinkled brightly, and he let out a laugh. "Oh, I am certain he has not."
A few days later, the Écho published a sensational article that read:
The historic Queen’s Necklace stolen from the Dreux-Soubise family has been returned to its owner by Arsène Lupin. Words of praise are not enough to commend such an honorable act.

People often ask me how I met Arsène Lupin, because I know so many intimate details about him. Some people wonder if I am the mysterious gentleman burglar. Well, I’m very flattered, but I am not he. However, I will tell you how I came to know him. In a word, it was chance.

On the evening of June 22, I was dining with some friends at one of Paris’ most charming restaurants. While the other patrons ate, danced, and laughed, our table was preoccupied with crimes, thefts, and unsolved mysteries. After dinner, my friend Jean Daspry and I said good-bye to our dinner companions, the Saint-Martins, and walked home.

When we arrived at the little house I’d been renting for a year, Daspry turned to me and said, "Aren’t afraid? Your house is so isolated. I would be frightened, especially after what we talked about all night."

I didn’t want to admit it, but I was a bit frightened. We shook hands, and I entered my dark, chilly home. I quickly ascended the stairs to my bedroom and locked the door. After lighting a candle, I found my revolver and placed it beside my bed. I changed, got into bed, and picked up my book from the night table. To my surprise, an envelope addressed to me fell out. I tore it open and read its contents: From the moment you read this letter, whatever happens, whatever you may hear, do not make a move or make a sound. If you do, you are doomed.

My heart pounded as I read and reread the letter. Was this some kind of joke? "This is nonsense!" I thought. "I’ll blow out my candle and go to sleep." But I could not do it. "Do not make a move," the letter had said. Suddenly, I heard the floor creak, and then a crackling noise. It was coming from the library, located two doors from my bedroom.
