I wanted to grab my gun, but I saw the window curtain move. I held my breath. It moved again; this time, I noticed a bulky mass that prevented the curtain from hanging straight. Someone was in my room, making sure I heeded the words of the letter. One movement, one sound, and I would be dead.

Throughout the night, I heard the most frightening noises coming from the library. It sounded like the walls were being torn down. Not knowing what was happening fueled the fear in me as I sat paralyzed in bed, my eyes fixed on the bulky curtain. Finally, the morning sun seeped through the window, and I heard the familiar bell of the milk wagon on the boulevard. That gave me courage to make my move. I grabbed my revolver, aimed at the curtain, and fired. I rushed to the window, but there was no one there! All night, I had been deceived by a fold in the curtain. Angry, I unlocked my door and ran to the library. Once again, I was stunned, for everything—furniture, books, pictures—was in its proper place. There was no trace of any intruders.
"This is unbelievable!" I shouted, rubbing my eyes.
Suddenly, something caught my eye. Sticking out from under a small Persian rug was a card—a playing card.

"It’s an ordinary seven of hearts," I said, picking it up. But I noticed something unusual. At the point of each of the seven hearts was a hole, as if the card had been pierced by a sharp object. I put the card in my pocket.

I spent the entire day in the library, carefully examining every inch of the room. It was an ornate room with mosaics on the walls. One image depicted a Roman god, and another showed a medieval king with a sword. There was a large window that a man could enter with the aid of a ladder, but the ladder would have made marks in the soft earth outside. There were no marks. Without evidence, I could not tell the police what had happened. Who would believe me? However, being a reporter for Gil Blas had its advantages. I wrote a lengthy account of the bizarre evening, and the paper published it the next day. Only Daspry seemed to take an interest in this strange affair; he quickly came to see me. I told him what had happened.
A few days later, I had an unexpected visitor. The gentleman would not give his name.
"I read your article in Gil Blas , and it interested me very much," he said.
"Thank you," I replied, leading him into the library.
"Are the facts you related exactly as they happened?" the man asked.
I nodded.
"Then you must leave me alone in this room," he said.
I looked at him in surprise.

"Certain details of your account bear an extraordinary resemblance to another case I’m familiar with. I can reveal further details only after I have determined for myself whether these two cases are connected. To do that, I must be alone," said the man nervously but firmly.
"How much time do you need?" I asked.
"Only three minutes," he replied.

I went downstairs, took out my watch, and began counting. One minute passed, and then two. I began to feel uneasy, so I started back up the stairs. Suddenly, I heard a gunshot. I raced to the library and found the man lying in the middle of the floor, a bullet wound in his forehead. His revolver lay close by, but another object near the body attracted my attention. It was a playing card—another seven of hearts. The pointed end of each heart also had a small, round hole.
Soon, the police arrived along with Monsieur Dudouis, chief of the Paris police.
"I did not touch the body," I explained and told them what had happened.
The preliminary examination was brief. The police searched the body, but there were no papers in the pockets of the deceased, no name on his clothes—nothing to give any clue to the man’s identity.

"Did this man come into my house just to commit suicide?" I thought. "There must have been something in this room that caused him to kill himself. What had he seen? What frightful secret had been revealed to him?"
"There is nothing missing from the room?" asked Dudouis.
"No, not that I can see," I said.
We watched silently as two policemen prepared to put the body on a stretcher. As they lifted the body, something fell from the left hand. It was a crumpled card.
"‘Georges Andermatt, 37, Rue de Berry, tel: 415.21,’" said Dudouis, reading the card.
"The Paris banker?" I asked. "This is he?"
Dudouis leaned over the body and shook his head. "No, Monsieur Andermatt is older, thinner. Do you have a telephone?"
"Of course. Come with me," I replied.
We went into the next room, and Dudouis dialed the number from the card.
"Monsieur Andermatt? This is Dudouis, chief of the Paris police. I request your presence, sir. Please come at once to 102 Boulevard Maillot. It is very important."
Monsieur Andermatt arrived twenty minutes later, and he was taken to see the body.
"He is Etienne Varin," Andermatt said in a low voice.
"You know him?" asked Monsieur Dudouis.
"Just by sight. I know his brother Alfred," said Andermatt. "He came to see me about a business matter once . . . I forget what it was."
"Do you know any reason why he would commit suicide?" asked Dudouis.
"No."
"He held your card in his hand," said Dudouis.
"I’m greatly surprised that my card was found here," Andermatt replied. "I have told you all I know. I sincerely hope this puzzle is cleared up during the investigation."

But the puzzle was not cleared up. The investigation established that the Varin brothers had led their lives under various names, frequented gambling resorts, and were possibly involved with a series of robberies. They hadn’t been seen for the last six years. The case seemed too complicated to me, so I decided not to waste any time on it. But my friend Daspry became more and more interested.
"Look at this," said Daspry, handing me a foreign newspaper a few days later. The paper provided an interesting piece of information, possibly connected to the suicide of Etienne Varin.
"‘The first trial of the new submarine will be launched in a secret location in the presence of the German emperor,’" I read aloud.
"That submarine was supposed to revolutionize naval warfare," Daspry said. "But, my friend, look at the name of the submarine!"
"The Seven-of-Hearts !" I exclaimed. "It also says here the submarine was designed by French engineers." I wondered if there was a connection to the events in my home.
Then Daspry showed me a copy of the Écho and said, "This article, titled ‘The Affair of the Seven-of-Hearts,’ was written by someone named Salvator, and it will shed light on this mysterious case."
Clearing his throat, he then read the entire article aloud. The story revealed that ten years ago, a young engineer named Louis Lacombe had rented number 102 Boulevard Maillot.
"That’s my house!" I interjected.
Daspry nodded and kept reading:

Lacombe was working on plans for a revolutionary submarine. The Varin brothers introduced Lacombe to Georges Andermatt, a banker with many government connections. Lacombe explained his submarine invention and Andermatt agreed to speak to the minister of the navy about buying Lacombe’s plans. For two years, Lacombe worked on his submarine, and he frequently visited the Andermatt home, growing closer to the family. Finally, Lacombe was ready to submit his work, and one evening, dined at the Andermatt home. He left there at eleven thirty and disappeared.
"What about the submarine plans?" I cried anxiously.
Daspry raised his finger to silence me and read on:
After much investigation, I, Salvator, have discovered that the plans for the Seven-of-Hearts ended up in the hands of the Varin brothers.
"But one of them is dead," I interrupted.
"The article goes on to say that the plans were sold to Germany, and the Seven-of-Hearts has already been constructed."
"Those scoundrels!" I exclaimed.

"Wait, my friend," said Daspry. "Salvator writes that the launch of the Seven-of-Hearts was not successful, and he adds, ‘It is believed the Varin brothers were missing a final document, and this was the document Lacombe had in his possession the night he disappeared. Without this document, the plans are incomplete and therefore worthless.’ The news story ends with a call for Andermatt to come forward and address these allegations."
"Who is Salvator?" I asked. "How does he know so much?"
Daspry shrugged and said, "Whoever he is, he is brave to bring these facts to the public’s attention."
After Salvator’s article appeared, an army of reporters descended upon the banker’s home, asking questions about his involvement in the suicide.
A few days later, Daspry and I were dining at my house when the door suddenly opened and a lady entered. She was wearing a veil.
"I apologize for this intrusion," she said before I had a chance to speak.
She went to the window and pulled the curtain closed. Her manner indicated she was familiar with the surroundings. But how could that be?
"I am here on an urgent matter," said the lady, raising her veil. "I am Madame Andermatt."
"Andermatt!" I cried, astonished.
"I have come hoping to obtain information."
"There’s nothing I can tell you," I said, "that hasn’t already been printed in the newspaper. I wish I could help . . ."
There was a moment of silence; she seemed embarrassed and nervous. Daspry suddenly stepped forward.
"May I ask a few personal questions?"
"Yes, you may," she said quietly.
"Did you know Louis Lacombe?"
Madame Andermatt’s face reddened. "He had business with my husband."
"When was the last time you saw him?" asked Daspry.
"The night he disappeared." She pressed a handkerchief to her eyes.
"Do you believe the Varin brothers had something to do with his disappearance?" Daspry continued.

"I am certain they did," she said. "When Louis, I mean, Monsieur Lacombe, left our house, he had his briefcase, which contained his papers. A few days later, my husband met with the Varins and discovered they had Louis’ papers. So they must have taken them from him."
"Why didn’t your husband tell the police?" I interrupted.
Madame Andermatt lowered her eyes. "There was something else in the briefcase."
"What?" I cried impatiently.

Daspry gave me a stern look and turned back to the woman. "The Varin brothers used the other item to blackmail your husband. Your husband, desiring to recover that item, was forced to keep silent about Lacombe and his papers."
The woman nodded sadly.
"That item," continued Daspry, "was a stack of love letters between you and Lacombe, was it not?"
I gasped loudly.

"Yes, and Alfred Varin threatened to publish them if my husband told anyone they had the plans," Madame Andermatt cried. "Varin said the letters were in a secret safe. But I believe my husband was able to discover that hiding place."
"Where is it?" I asked.
"Here."
"Here?" I repeated.

"Louis Lacombe was a genius and amused himself by designing safes and locks during his leisure time. My husband believed the Varin brothers used one of Lacombe’s safes to conceal the papers and letters."
"You mean the plans and letters are here?" I said, in wonderment.

"Not now," she said. "I believe my husband recovered them on the night of June 22. He came to this house, opened the safe, and left his card to inform the brothers he feared them no more. Two days later, after reading the article in Gil Blas , Etienne Varin came, found the safe empty, and killed himself."
Daspry thought a moment and then said, "A good theory, madame, but it was not your husband who entered this house on June 22."
"Who, then?" she exclaimed.
"There is a mysterious individual who is managing this affair. He holds the answers in his hand. It was he and his friends who entered this house that night and discovered the safe."
"Daspry, who is it?" I asked insistently.
"The one who has revealed convincing details no one else could know and the one who has discovered the secrets of the Varin brothers. The same one who published his findings in the Écho : Salvator!"
Madame Andermatt became upset when Daspry mentioned Salvator. "He has my letters!" she cried. "What am I to do?"

"Write to him," urged Daspry. "Say that your husband has the document that completes the submarine plans—because I believe your husband does possess that document. Confide in Salvator. Tell him you need your letters."

Madame thanked us and promised to keep us informed. Two days later, she sent us a note she had received: Have not found the letters, but I will get them. Rest easy. I am watching everything. – Salvator
The handwriting was the same as that in the note I had found in my book on June 22.
"You’re right," I told Daspry. "Salvator is managing this affair."
Daspry smiled modestly. "Soon, we will unravel this mystery."
"But what about the two playing cards?" I asked.
"I’m not concerned about those now," said Daspry. "I must find Madame Andermatt’s letters!"
For days, Daspry furiously searched the house, inside and out, but he found nothing. Then, one day, he came to me with a pickax and shovel.
"Come," he ordered, and we began digging behind the house. We labored for an hour without success. I was discouraged and wanted to give up when Daspry suddenly cried out. "At last!"

His pickax had hit some bones, the remains of a skeleton with scraps of clothing still hanging from it. I felt sick to my stomach. Next to the bones was a small, rectangular iron plate. He picked it up and scraped the dirt off.
"It’s the exact size of a playing card," I remarked. The plate had red spots, and each spot was pierced with a round hole in the same position as the holes on the sevens of hearts we had found.

I felt unwell after the discovery of the skeleton, so I rested for a few days while Daspry continued his search for the letters in the library. For hours, he would tap, tap, tap on the walls, hoping to find the secret hiding place.

On the morning of the third day, I received a curious letter. The drama that began on June 22 is now moving forward. Circumstances force me to bring the two principal players together. The meeting will take place in your house, tonight at nine o’clock, with your permission. – Salvator
That night, Daspry arrived at eight o’clock, and I showed him the letter.
Daspry laughed heartily and said, "Oh, we must stay and see what happens, my friend."
We made sure the doors were unlocked, and at 8:40, the doorbell rang.
"They’re early!" remarked Daspry.
I went to the door and found Madame Andermatt.

"My husband is coming," she gasped, rushing in. "They intend to give him the letters." She explained that a servant had given a message for her husband to her by mistake. "He grabbed it from me, but I had read it already. He was told to come here tonight and bring the document connected with the project. In exchange, he’ll receive the letters."
"Does your husband know you are here?" Daspry asked.
She shook her head. Suddenly, the clock struck nine.
"Quickly!" I whispered, leading the others to a velvet curtain in the library. "We can hide behind here but observe the events of the room." Within moments, we heard the front door creak open.
"Not a word," Daspry warned.

Someone entered the library. I peeked around the curtain and saw Alfred Varin. I recognized him because he resembled his brother. Varin scrutinized the room carefully, his eyes lingering on the mosaic of the king and his sword. Suddenly, the door swung open.
"You! You brought me here?" Monsieur Andermatt bellowed as he entered the room.
"You sent for me!" shouted Varin.
"No," declared Andermatt.
"Someone has lured us both here," said Varin. "I’m leaving."
"Wait!" shouted Andermatt, blocking Varin’s way. "What happened to Lacombe?"
"How should I know?" spat Varin.
"Because a few days after he disappeared, you had the submarine plans and tried to sell them to me. How did you get them?" demanded Andermatt.
Varin smiled wickedly. "All you care about are your wife’s letters. No?"
Andermatt’s face grew red. "Yes. Give them to me."
"Only if you give me the final document for the submarine," Varin said coldly. He reached into his coat pocket, drew a revolver, and pointed it at Andermatt. "Hand them over."
Suddenly, a pistol shot sounded, and Varin’s weapon dropped to the floor. Daspry had fired, and in a moment, he was standing between the two men.
"Who are you?" Varin gasped.
"The one holding the cards," said Daspry, holding up the iron plate with the red spots. "You were told to bring something?"
Varin took out a large envelope. "I want twenty thousand francs for the plans."
"Monsieur Andermatt will kindly sign a check in the amount of ten thousand francs," said Daspry. Andermatt began to protest, but then obediently wrote out the check. "Now, the package of letters."
"I haven’t got them," Varin replied.
"No?" said Daspry. "Open the hiding place." Daspry held out the iron plate.
Varin shook his head vehemently.

"Then I shall." Daspry walked toward the mosaic of the king. He lined up the iron plate with the edges of the king’s sword, and then punched through its seven holes with an awl he had in his pocket, pressing on seven of the mosaic’s stones. There was a clicking sound, and a part of the wall opened, leaving a large opening.
"It’s a safe!" I thought.
"It’s empty," said Varin smugly. "And there is no other hiding place."
"There must be. Where is it?" demanded Daspry.
Varin thought a moment and replied, "I want another ten thousand francs."
"You’ll have it," said Andermatt and signed another check.
Varin took the plate from Daspry, closed the safe, turned the plate around, and placed it on the sword again. There was another clicking sound, and a smaller safe opened.
Inside the small safe was a packet of letters.
"Did you bring the final document for the submarine, the Seven-of-Hearts?" asked Daspry.
Andermatt nodded and handed the paper and checks to Daspry.
"Then our business has ended," said Daspry as he gave Andermatt the letters. The banker left without a backward glance.
"My money, monsieur," grumbled Varin.
"The money is mine now," Daspry replied coolly.
Varin’s face turned purple, but he remained calm. "Might I ask you a question?"
"You may."
"Was there a black case in the large safe?"
Daspry nodded. "I found it on June 22."
"Did you take it?" Varin’s voice shook.
"It was filled with jewels," said Daspry. "Of course I took it."
"What is your name?" asked Varin, shaking his head.
Daspry glanced over at where I was hiding. "Arsène Lupin."
Varin looked stunned as he staggered out the door.
"Daspry, I mean Lupin—oh, what do I call you?" I cried, coming out of hiding. "Madame Andermatt has fainted."
We rushed over to her just as she was regaining consciousness.
"My letters . . . ," she said in a small voice.

"Do not worry, madame," whispered Lupin, taking a package out of his pocket. "These are your real letters. I gave your husband fake letters that will not incriminate you. Go home. Your husband will be happy to see you."
Madame Andermatt clutched the letters and hurried out the door.
"I have many questions," I said when we were alone.
"And I am ready to answer them, my friend," Lupin said, as we left the library together.
The next morning, an article appeared in the Écho :

Arsène Lupin has solved the mystery submitted by Salvator. Having acquired all the documents for Lacombe’s submarine, he has placed them in the hands of the minister of the navy. He has also made a generous donation in the sum of twenty thousand francs for the construction of the submarine.
And that is how I made the acquaintance of Arsène Lupin, gentleman burglar, but more importantly, my dear friend.

Late one winter night, Monsieur Imbert was walking home from a party, his footsteps echoing pleasantly. But soon, he got the feeling someone was following him. Imbert turned around and thought he saw a shadow behind a tree, so he quickened his steps. Suddenly, Imbert was attacked from behind. He shouted for help, but his attacker was too strong and pinned him to the ground. Luckily, a passerby rushed to help and fought off the assailant.
"Are you hurt, sir?" the rescuer asked, helping Imbert to his feet.
Imbert was too shaken to walk, so the man waved down a cab, helped him into the vehicle, and accompanied Imbert home.
"I owe you my life," said Imbert as they arrived at his mansion. "My wife is asleep, but she will want to thank you for your heroism. Please come to lunch tomorrow. My name is Ludovic Imbert."
"I am Arsène Lupin," replied the man.

Lupin was not yet famous; in fact, it was for this particular affair that the gentleman burglar invented this name. With the help of an associate, Lupin had planned this attack for six months, collecting information on the Imberts and questioning their servants. Finally, his goal was within reach. Soon, Lupin would be in the Imbert home and near their safe, which was rumored to contain stocks and bonds worth millions!
The next day, Lupin arrived at the mansion and met Gervaise, Imbert's plump and talkative wife.
"Welcome, Monsieur Lupin," she gushed.

The Imberts and Lupin spent lunch getting acquainted, and by the time dessert was served, Lupin knew everything about them. Madame Imbert had inherited millions from a rich friend named Andrew Brawford, but his nephews were challenging her inheritance.
"The bonds and stocks are in our safe," she lamented, "but we can't sell them until the legalities are resolved."
"So the rumors are true," Lupin thought, thrilled at his proximity to the safe.

Out of gratitude, the Imberts appointed Lupin as their personal secretary when their new friend confessed to being somewhat poor. Lupin was given an office on the second floor, directly above Imbert's office and the safe. But Lupin noticed quickly that his position involved very little actual work. In two months, he wrote only four letters and was never called into his employer's office. He never socialized with the Imberts, and the servants didn't talk to him. Lupin did not complain, since he preferred to spend his time working on a plan. He made secret visits to Imbert's office to inspect the safe, a large block of iron that could only be opened with both a combination and a key.

"Where force fails, cunning prevails," Lupin said to himself. He bored a hole through the floor of his room to penetrate the ceiling of Imbert's office. Then he inserted a pipe through the hole so he could see and hear what transpired in the room below. Stretched out on the floor, Lupin often saw the couple in front of the safe, examining books and papers. Whenever they twisted the combination lock, Lupin watched, trying to learn the numbers. One day, the couple left the office without locking the safe, and Lupin quickly went downstairs. On entering the room, however, he saw they had abruptly returned.
"I beg your pardon," Lupin said deftly. "I must have opened the wrong door."
Gervaise ran up to him. "Come in, I'm glad you're here."
"We want your advice," murmured Imbert. "Should we sell some of the bonds or stocks?"
"But I thought Brawford's nephews prevented you from selling," said Lupin, surprised.
"Oh, their lawsuit doesn't involve all our holdings," answered Gervaise. The shelves inside the safe were filled with bundles of stocks and bonds, and she took one out.
"Not those stocks, Gervaise," her husband protested. "They're not selling well right now. But the government bonds might turn a profit. What do you think, Lupin?"

"I agree with you," said Lupin, even though he had no idea which ones to sell or keep. But that afternoon, Imbert and Lupin sold some of the bonds for 46,000 francs. "Imagine how much money all of them would fetch!" thought Lupin.

To complicate matters, stories accusing the Imberts of being swindlers appeared in the press, which threw the entire household into uncertainty. Lupin decided he must act, or he would lose everything.

During the next five days, instead of leaving the mansion at six o'clock as usual, Lupin would lock himself in his office. He lay on the floor, watching Imbert's office, hoping for a chance to steal the stocks and bonds. On the sixth day, Lupin got his chance. The couple, upset by the press accounts, decided to review the safe's contents. Lupin spied on them for hours that evening, and when the servants went to bed, Lupin decided to make his move.
"It's now or never," he murmured.
Using a knotted rope, he climbed out of his window and quietly dropped down to the balcony of the office window below.
"I'm tired," Gervaise complained.
"Don't worry. I'll finish up," said her husband.
Earlier, Lupin had unlocked the office windows so he could enter easily. When he heard Gervaise leave, he opened the window slightly, and the curtain billowed with the night breeze.
"It's cold in here," Imbert remarked and rose to close the window.

As soon as Imbert neared the window, Lupin wrapped the man's head in the curtain and tied him up before Imbert could see his assailant. Then, Lupin ran to the open safe and put the bundles of stocks and bonds into a cloth sack he had previously hidden. He raced upstairs to his office, removed the rope, and covered the hole in the floor. Lupin exited through the servant's gate, where a carriage was waiting for him.
Examining the bundles a few hours later , Lupin said to his associate, "These won't add up to millions, but we'll still collect a respectable sum."
The next morning, Lupin read a startling headline in the newspaper.
"'Ludovic and Gervaise Imbert have disappeared,'" read Lupin aloud. The police had raided the Imbert mansion only moments after Lupin had left and found the home empty.
These are the facts as Arsène Lupin related them to me much later, pacing nervously up and down in my study.
"There are some things I still don't understand about this affair," he confided. "For example, why did the Imberts flee? They could have said they were robbed. The safe was empty."
"Did you ever see them again?" I asked.
Lupin shook his head.
"Maybe you're feeling regret," I said. "You stole their fortune."
"What fortune?" Lupin shouted. "All their stocks and bonds were counterfeit! Fakes! The Imberts played me for a fool!"
I stared at him, dumbfounded.

"Unknown to me, I was playing a role from the very beginning. Reading the newspapers after their disappearance, I realized they had been passing me off as one of Andrew Brawford's nephews," said Lupin. "You see, they told their acquaintances that the lawsuit was over. No one knew my real name or quite what I did there. So, thanks to my existence, the Imberts were able to borrow money from everyone."
"Because they thought the Imberts would soon be able to access their funds!" I added, finally understanding how the couple's scheme worked.

"And worst of all, that woman borrowed 1,500 francs from me! I gave her my life savings willingly, thinking I would steal millions from her in return . . ." Lupin sat down and buried his face in his hands.
"Are you all right, old chap?" I asked, worried.

Then my friend raised his head and burst into laughter at the great joke that had been played on him. The novice gentleman burglar had learned a valuable lesson on his way to becoming the great Arsène Lupin.
The doorbell awakened the guard of the quiet apartment building. He glanced at his watch. It was three o'clock in the morning.
"It must be an emergency for the doctor on the third floor," he murmured as he got up to open the door for the visitor.
Once inside, the visitor silently ascended the stairs, and without stopping at the third floor, proceeded up to the fifth floor. There he tried two keys in the lock. One of them fit.

"Perfect," he said, and he waited a few minutes before descending to the lobby. "That's enough time for the guard to assume I have seen the doctor," he thought. The visitor exited the building noisily so the guard would believe he had left, but he stuck something in the lock so it would not bolt. A few minutes later, he quietly entered again, went up to the fifth floor, and sneaked into the dark apartment. He took out a floor plan of the apartment and shined a flashlight on it.

"This corridor leads to the bedrooms," he thought. "A closet door connects to the countess' bedroom." He turned off the flashlight and walked to the closet. He was about to pick the lock, but the door opened easily. "You are lucky, Lupin," he whispered to himself. He stepped inside the closet and easily picked the lock on the door leading to the bedroom. "According to the floor plan," thought Lupin, "there's a small table by the bed. The black pearl will be inside a box of stationery on that table."

The Countess Zalti, whose bedroom floor Lupin now was creeping across, had once been the most admired woman in Paris. She had owned exquisite jewelry, worn fine clothes, and traveled to exotic places, but then lost her fortune and now had just a small apartment, a manservant, and a housekeeper. To sustain herself, she had sold all her jewels except for the famous black pearl. It was worth more than all the other jewels combined, and she would not part with it.
Lupin had almost reached the table when his fingers touched something on the floor.
"An overturned candlestick? Strange!" he thought. Then his hand brushed against something else—hair, and after that an ice-cold face. Lupin froze and nearly screamed.

"Countess Zalti," he whispered. He quickly turned on his flashlight, stood up, and surveyed the room. He saw signs of a struggle—an overturned chair, a small clock with its hands stopped at 11:20. Then, his heart beating wildly, he saw the countess lying motionless on the floor, with a red gash across her neck. Blood was everywhere.
"She's dead," thought Lupin. Then he remembered the black pearl and looked in the box of stationery. It was empty! Lupin collapsed onto a chair to think. Forty minutes later he left the building.

Countess Zalti and her famous black pearl were once again in the newspapers—this time, however, because of her gruesome murder. The newspapers reported that her manservant, Victor Danègre, had been arrested. Upon searching his room, the chief of police, Dudouis, had found a coat stained with a few drops of blood hidden under his mattress. Later a missing button from that coat was found under the countess' bed. However, some points needed further explanation. Witnesses said Danègre went to a tobacco shop at seven o'clock in the morning. But the countess' housekeeper testified that the door was locked when she rose at eight o'clock. Danègre did not have a key, so how did he leave the apartment and lock the door after himself?

The police's investigation turned up no answers—only new mysteries. The countess' cousin declared that a month before her death, the countess had written to her and described the exact location of the black pearl. That letter, however, had disappeared the next day. The building's guard recalled a visitor for the doctor, but the doctor testified he had seen no one. There were too many suspects in the case and not enough evidence, so the police had to free Danègre.

During the six-month investigation, Danègre had been in prison. Upon release he was physically and mentally weak, a shadow of his former self. Because of the publicity, he couldn't get a job, so he changed his name to Anatole Dufour.
One evening, as he was eating dinner at a cafe, a man wearing a black raincoat entered and sat at his table. The man poured them both some wine.
"To your health, Victor Danègre," the man toasted.
"You are mistaken. My name is Dufour."
The man shook his head and said, "I am Grimaudan, ex-detective, and you are Victor Danègre, ex-servant of the deceased Countess Zalti."
"What do you want?" growled Danègre.
"I've been sent by the countess' cousin," replied Grimaudan, "to recover the black pearl."
"I don't have it," said Danègre.
"Oh yes, you do," Grimaudan retorted.
"The police couldn't prove it," insisted Danègre.
Grimaudan took a sip of wine.
"Three weeks before the murder, you took the countess' key and paid the locksmith to make a copy."
"That's a lie!" shouted Danègre.
Grimaudan took the key out of his pocket.
"You killed the countess with a knife you bought from a shop the same day you duplicated the key," continued Grimaudan.
"No!" cried Danègre.
Again Grimaudan reached into his pocket. He took out the knife.
"You have a key and a knife. Who can prove they belong to me?" said Danègre, regaining his composure.
"The locksmith and the clerk at the shop will identify you," replied Grimaudan coldly.
Danègre's mouth went dry. "It's been too long. They could never remember all their customers."
"Perhaps. But there is more evidence that will convict you of this terrible crime—your fingerprint."
Danègre started to argue, but Grimaudan continued.

"After you murdered the countess, you left through the closet. You were scared, unsteady, and leaned against the wall for support. Your thumb, wet with blood, made an impression on the wall. If I direct the police to that fingerprint, they will see it matches yours."
Danègre hung his head. "How much will you give me for the pearl?"
"Nothing," replied Grimaudan. "I will give you your life."
"I will take you to it," said Danègre.
They walked out of the restaurant and toward the countess' former apartment building, finally stopping in front of a bench.
"It's here."
"Where?" Grimaudan looked around but didn't see anything.
Danègre remained silent.
"You still want me to pay you for the pearl," Grimaudan remarked. "How much?"
"Just enough to get me to America," Danègre replied.
"Agreed," said Grimaudan. "Now where is it?"
"See the pavement stones? Count the stones to the right of the sewer grate. The pearl is between the twelfth and thirteenth stones."

Grimaudan counted the stones. When he got to the spot, he took out a knife and thrust it between the stones, digging deeply. His knife struck something, and he enlarged the hole with his finger. Finally Grimaudan pulled the pearl out of its filthy hiding place.
The following day the Écho printed this article:
Yesterday the famous black pearl fell into the hands of Arsène Lupin, who
acquired it from the murderer of the Countess Zalti. Soon the precious jewel
will be exhibited around the world for all to admire. Lupin is prepared to
receive offers for the jewel.
Lupin and I discussed the affair over dinner one evening.

"I had enough time in the countess' bedroom to form a plan to catch the murderer and retrieve the black pearl," explained Lupin. "I decided that Danègre had to be arrested but not convicted. So I made sure the police found Danègre's button, but not the knife and key. I also wiped off the fingerprint in the closet."
"And poor Danègre fell right into your trap," I said.
"And this fell right into my hands." Lupin's eyes twinkled as he held up the black pearl.
"Meet Arsène Lupin!" joked Georges Devanne, a wealthy banker, as he presented Horace Velmont, a friend.
The introduction was met with laughter by his guests, who were at Thibermesnil Castle.
"There is an uncanny resemblance," remarked Father Gelis, one of the guests. "But I did hear that Lupin has been spotted in this area."
The gentleman who was the object of their laughter did in fact look rather like Lupin. He stood quietly, wearing a bemused smile.

"I first met Velmont," Devanne continued, nodding toward his smiling friend, "three months ago at a casino in Dieppe. He is a talented painter, and my brother knows his work well. He has visited my home several times since then, but he has never crept around in the middle of the night. At least I don't think so."

This speech provoked another eruption of laughter, and then the guests followed Devanne into the gallery, which occupied the entire first floor of the castle. This gallery contained Devanne's growing collection of antiques and paintings, plus an immense bookcase. At the top of the bookcase, the name of the castle was spelled out in gold: Thibermesnil. After the guests lit their cigars, Devanne resumed the conversation.
"Velmont, if you are going to rob me, tonight is your last chance."
"Why is that?" Velmont grinned.
Devanne took a sip of his wine before answering casually, "I'm expecting a visitor tomorrow afternoon at four o'clock—Sherlock Holmes, the famous English detective."
At first the guests were speechless; then they began asking questions all at once.
"Is Holmes really coming?"
"Is Lupin truly in the neighborhood?"
"Did you get a warning letter like Baron Cahorn?"

Devanne laughed. "Lupin and his band are not far away, I suspect," said Devanne. "And Lupin would not use the same trick twice. However, I know he's up to something. That's why I sent for the great detective himself."
"What's Lupin planning?" asked Velmont.

Devanne walked to the bookcase and said, "These books contain the history of the Thibermesnil family." Then he pointed to an empty space on the shelf. "As you can see, one book is missing—the book detailing the construction of the castle. That volume describes a secret underground tunnel, with an entrance somewhere in this room. The book disappeared a month ago."
"A lost book hardly seems a sufficient reason for summoning Sherlock Holmes," commented Velmont.

"Ordinarily I would agree," said Devanne, "but there was another copy in the National Library in Paris, which contained details about the secret tunnel not included in my book. In other words, one would need both books in order to determine the exact location of the tunnel."
"Let me guess," interjected Velmont. "That book has also disappeared."
Devanne nodded.
"And you believe Lupin is behind this?" asked Father Gelis.
"Yes. When I explained the situation to Holmes, he was eager to match wits with Arsène Lupin," Devanne replied.
"What an honor for Lupin," said Velmont. "But what if Lupin is not planning to rob you?"
"Holmes is also interested in solving the mystery of the secret tunnel," said Devanne.
"Can you remember anything about the tunnel from the missing book?" asked Velmont.

Devanne nodded. "For centuries the castle lords waited until they lay on their deathbeds to pass on the tunnel's location to their sons. The last of the lords of Thibermesnil was beheaded in the French Revolution at the age of 19, and he had no children. Since then others, including me, have tried to find the tunnel—without success. The house plans in the book at the National Library showed a series of stairs with a total of 48 steps, which descend more than ten meters."
"That would mean the tunnel runs underneath the old moat surrounding this castle ," exclaimed Velmont.
"And ends within the walls of this room," said Devanne. "But where exactly does it lie? The mystery remains."
"Do not forget the two quotations, Monsieur Devanne," prompted Father Gelis.
Devanne laughed. "Father Gelis has been interested in Thibermesnil for many years. He came across a cryptic quote in the church archives. But I must say, it only confuses the matter."
"What's the quote?" asked Velmont.

"Well, legend has it that Henry IV spent a night in this castle just before a famous battle," began Devanne. "His mistress was brought to him through the tunnel. The king confided the secret location to his minister, saying, ‘Turn one eye on the bee that shakes; the other eye will lead to God.'"
"It doesn't make sense," said Velmont.
"It's code, monsieur," Father Gelis said hotly. "Obviously Henry IV did not want anyone to know the whereabouts of the secret tunnel."
"Father Gelis also discovered a note in Louis XVI's famous jewelry chest in the Louvre; it read ‘Thibermesnil 3-4-11,'" said Devanne.
"Ah! The magic key," Velmont said sarcastically. "Now, who can fit the key into the invisible lock?"
Father Gelis stiffened his shoulders. "Laugh as much as you like, but I'm confident those two clues are the key to the location of the tunnel."
"Sherlock Holmes will figure it out, I'm sure," added Devanne.
Velmont shook Devanne's hand. "I think your book and the one in the library lacked a very important detail," he said, smiling broadly, "which you just supplied. Now I can plunder your castle."
"You'll have to hurry, Monsieur Lupin ." Devanne chuckled. "Sherlock Holmes arrives tomorrow."
"Then it shall have to be tonight," Velmont replied with a wink.
"By the way, I can drive you to Dieppe this evening," Devanne said. "I am meeting some friends and a young lady they know at the train station. They will be staying with me."
An hour later Devanne and Velmont were driving toward Dieppe. Devanne dropped off Velmont and then picked up his friends at the train station.

The castle remained in darkness until the clock struck three in the morning. Suddenly there was a clicking noise in the gallery, and a thin stream of light flashed from the bookcase. Then the room flooded with light as a whole section of the bookcase rotated to reveal a large opening.

Arsène Lupin walked into the room carrying a flashlight, followed by eight men carrying various tools and a coil of rope. Lupin passed quickly from one piece of furniture to another and instructed his accomplices whether to take it or leave it. In just forty minutes, the best pieces from the room had been removed in an orderly and noiseless manner, and the men exited the same way they had entered. Lupin pushed the bookcase back into place after them and carefully removed all traces of the men's footsteps and fingerprints from the gallery.

Next he walked down a corridor to a glass cabinet containing a priceless collection of watches, rings, and figurines. Lupin picked the lock and began to fill his pockets with the miniature treasures, but a faint noise startled him. He remembered there was a guest room at the end of the corridor, where one of the friends Devanne had picked up that evening was probably sleeping.

Lupin quickly extinguished his flashlight and had just hidden behind a curtain when the guest-room door opened. Lupin saw a woman walking down the corridor. She appeared nervous; the candle she carried shook slightly. She passed so close that her skirt brushed against the curtain and he could smell her perfume. Then, without warning, she stopped and pulled the curtain aside. Lupin was dumbstruck.
"Miss Nelly," he whispered.

Arsène Lupin was frozen in place. Standing before him was the lovely Miss Nelly! The same charming creature who, rather than betray him on the ship, had dropped the camera hiding the diamonds into the water.
"I dreamed of seeing you again one day," Lupin finally said.
Her eyes moved to his hands, which were filled with jewelry. She shuddered and ran into the gallery.
"Please, I can explain," cried Lupin, embarrassed to be caught like a common thief.
He followed and found her trembling at the sight of the devastated room.
"Tomorrow, at three o'clock, everything will be returned," he said. "I promise."
Suddenly she spoke. "Listen . . . footsteps. You must go." She ran toward the door to the gallery and listened. When she turned around, Arsène Lupin was gone.
Early the next morning, Devanne was informed about the robbery, and he immediately thought, "Velmont is Lupin!" But then he reconsidered. "It's ridiculous to suspect the famous painter."
The police could find no clues—except one. The castle's missing book had been restored to the bookcase, and next to it was the book missing from the National Library.

Devanne's friends arrived at 11 o'clock to provide support and to satisfy their curiosity; the only friend not present was Velmont, which aroused Devanne's suspicions again. But the suspected thief appeared at noon.
"Velmont!" Devanne cried.
"Surprised to see me?" Velmont asked innocently.
"Yes, since you robbed me last night," said Devanne.
"Nonsense!" exclaimed Velmont pleasantly.
He was introduced to Devanne's new guests and Miss Nelly and smiled at her, but she coolly turned away.

Devanne ushered his guests onto the terrace overlooking the entrance to the castle. They talked about the robbery and the imminent arrival of Holmes. At twenty minutes to three, Miss Nelly remembered Lupin's promise and couldn't help glancing at the clock. Finally the clock struck three. Two wagons appeared and stopped beneath the terrace.
A police officer called out, "Monsieur Devanne, we have located your belongings."
Excited, Devanne and his guests ran outside. He peered under the wagon covers to behold his stolen treasures.
"We received an anonymous note telling us where to find them," explained the officer.
During the commotion Miss Nelly had remained on the terrace. But she was not alone.
"I kept my promise," Lupin whispered.
She just stood there, silent.
"Forget that I'm a thief," he begged. "Remember those wonderful days when I was Bernard d'Andrézy. Please?"
She pointed to a ring on his finger. The ring belonged to Georges Devanne.
"You are right." He smiled bitterly. "Arsène Lupin is now and always will be Arsène Lupin."
He bowed as she walked away, never to see her again.
"I must leave before Sherlock Holmes arrives," he thought, running out a back door and through the woods behind the castle. Back on the road, he soon encountered a tall man carrying a cane.
"Excuse me, is this the way to the castle?" the man asked in an English accent.
"Yes," replied Lupin. "They are expecting you, Mr. Holmes."

Sherlock Holmes scrutinized Lupin from head to foot. Suddenly two policemen on horses galloped by, forcing the two men into the bushes to avoid being trampled. The two remarkable men emerged and brushed themselves off. Then, without a word, they parted and went their separate ways—two opposing forces of nature that had been destined to meet face-to-face for just a moment.
"Ah, you are here. I am delighted to meet you!" cried Devanne when Holmes walked up to the castle. "Did my chauffeur meet you at the station?"
"I preferred to walk," grumbled Holmes.
Devanne forced a smile and proceeded to explain the events of the night before. Holmes turned to leave.
"Where are you going?" asked Devanne.
"Home," the Englishman replied.
"But why?"
"Your goods have been returned and Lupin is gone. There is nothing for me to do."
"But I need your help!" Devanne cried. "We do not know how he got in or why he returned the goods."
Holmes removed his hat and said, "Tell me everything."
Devanne escorted the detective to the gallery, showed him the returned books, and explained about the secret tunnel. Holmes asked questions about everything.
"Was yesterday the first time you spoke about the two quotes?" Holmes asked.
"Yes," replied Devanne.

"Prepare to take me back to the station in an hour," Holmes said confidently. "That is how long it took Lupin to solve this mystery, and so it shall be with me." He paced the room, in deep thought, and then sat down and closed his eyes. After a few minutes, he said, "Is there a chapel near the castle?"
"Yes, but—"
"Tell your driver to wait for me there," interrupted Holmes.
"Do you think the tunnel runs to the chapel?" asked Devanne, ignoring Holmes' request.
"Now, bring me a ladder and a flashlight," ordered Holmes.
Devanne rushed to provide what the detective requested.
"Place the ladder against the bookcase to the left of the word ‘Thibermesnil,'" he instructed.
Devanne obeyed.
"Climb up and turn the first letter I ," Holmes continued.
"It turns to the right," Devanne cried excitedly.
"Take the letter B and move it back and forth," ordered Holmes.
When Devanne did that, there was a clicking sound.
"Now, move the ladder to the other end of the word 'Thibermesnil' and pull the other letter I ," said Holmes.
Devanne pulled the letter, and an entire section of the bookcase opened, pushing him off the ladder.
Unhurt, Devanne stared into the dark opening. "The secret tunnel!"

"Turn one eye on the bee that shakes; the other eye will lead to God," said Holmes. "Turn the first I in Thibermesnil, shake the B , then pull the other I . Just to remind himself, Louis XVI wrote 3-4-11 . . . the third, fourth, and eleventh letters of the name."
Devanne gazed at Holmes with admiration as the detective stepped into the tunnel.
"From inside here the reverse side of the letters can be reached," Holmes said. "Lupin worked the combination that way to get inside."
"Then he knows the other entrance," cried Devanne.
"Yes, and I do too," said Holmes as he continued down the tunnel, with Devanne following.

First they descended a stairway of 48 steps and then walked through a long, damp passageway. At last the men came to another stairway of 48 steps and ascended to a granite wall, which Holmes examined.

"Aha!" he exclaimed when he saw the word "Thibermesnil" in reverse on the wall. Holmes used the same combination, and the large block of granite opened into the old chapel. On the other side, the granite formed a tomb with the word "Thibermesnil" engraved on it.
"The other eye leads to God," said Holmes. "This chapel."
Devanne clapped his hands excitedly. The two men emerged from the chapel to find Devanne's automobile waiting for them.
"How did you know to come here?" Devanne asked the driver.
"Monsieur Velmont told me," answered the man.
"He knew you would solve the mystery," said Devanne to Holmes.
A smile of satisfaction lit up the detective's face. "I knew Lupin was clever when I saw him."
"You saw Lupin?" asked Devanne.
"On my way to the castle," Holmes replied.
"You didn't stop him?" exclaimed Devanne.
Ignoring him, Holmes got into the automobile and saw a package addressed to him on the seat.
"What is it?" asked Devanne.
Holmes opened the package, took out a watch, and frowned. He recalled the horses forcing him and Lupin into the bushes.
Devanne began laughing. "Arsène Lupin stole your watch. Now he returns it!"
"Yes, he is a clever man," Holmes said. "And one day I shall have the pleasure of meeting him again. Yes, Sherlock Holmes will meet Arsène Lupin again."
